talks.title: BlueHat 2026: From trusted agents to adversaries: Securing agentic AI in the age of prompt injection
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of BlueHat 2026: From trusted agents to adversaries: Securing agentic AI in the age of prompt injection.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Jason Martin (Director of Adversarial Research, Hidden Layer) and Abash present research on securing AI agents against prompt injection attacks. The talk combines offensive demonstrations with defensive strategies, explaining why agentic AI systems are fundamentally difficult to secure and proposing a multi-layered defense approach centered on treating agents as managed insider threats.

## Key Topics

**OpenClaw Attack Case Study**
The speakers demonstrate a real indirect prompt injection attack against OpenClaw, a highly capable open-source AI agent. By crafting a malicious website with hidden instructions and control sequences, they compromised the agent, injected code into its heartbeat.mmd file (a recurring task mechanism), and established persistent command-and-control with 30-minute polling intervals. The agent faithfully checked for new instructions even after the researcher forgot to tear down the attack.

**Why AI Security is Fundamentally Hard**
Large language models are inherently probabilistic systems with exponential choice spaces (e.g., 128K vocabulary to the power of 200K context window). Unlike deterministic systems with well-defined protocols, AI models learn spurious correlations from training data and lack structural boundaries between instruction types. Role separation relies on probabilistic primitives—role markers, positional encoding, and attention mechanisms—which are designed to guide behavior, not prevent mixing. This makes instruction hierarchy enforcement inherently fragile.

**Prompt Injection & Instruction Hierarchy**
Current LLM implementations concatenate system instructions, user input, and tool responses into a single token stream using control tokens for textual separation. These separations are purely probabilistic hints, not structural barriers. The core vulnerability: text from any source (especially untrusted tool responses or web content) can be interpreted as system-level instructions, enabling injection attacks. Techniques include control sequence manipulation to trigger reasoning modes and cognitive manipulation through multi-step reasoning injection.

**Agent as Insider Threat**
Once compromised, an agent resembles a trusted insider: it can execute code, access data, call APIs, persist across sessions, and write its own code payloads. The Klein CI/CD example showed how a triage agent with bash access could be pivoted into supply-chain compromise—stealing credentials, publishing unauthorized packages, and deploying OpenClaw for further attack orchestration.

**Defense Architecture**
The speakers outline defense across four pillars:
- **Identity**: Deterministic, least-privilege enforcement; no LLM-inferred permissions; continuous behavior verification
- **Data**: Treat all external data as untrusted; evaluate trustworthiness continuously; track provenance
- **Access & Monitoring**: Sandboxing; anomaly detection; C2 pattern recognition in tool invocation pipelines
- **Human Accountability**: Subject matter experts (not rubber-stamp approvers) responsible for consequential actions; non-repudiation and traceability required

Blast radius scales with agent tool capabilities; the mitigation is both constraining tools and monitoring behavior across layered defense.

## Technical Details

**Attack Mechanism**: The OpenClaw attack used control sequences (reserved token sequences) to split a tool response and break out of the fetch tool call into a reasoning/thinking mode. Injected text claiming "no dry run" argument was present created a false reasoning trace, convincing the model to execute a downloaded script. That script inserted a heartbeat instruction pointing to the attacker's C2 server.

**Instruction Hierarchy Reality vs. Theory**: Theory posits alignment > system/developer instructions > user instructions > tool responses. Practice squishes all into one token stream with only control tokens as visual markers. Role markers, positional encoding, and attention are probabilistic separators, not structural enforcement.

**Model Probabilistic Nature**: With exponential choice spaces and no structural role boundaries, prediction of model behavior is fundamentally intractable. Temperature tuning and context manipulation are weak defenses against determined attackers exploiting the many probability paths.

## Takeaways

1. **Threat Model**: Treat compromised agents like compromised insiders, not malware. Apply identity/access/monitoring practices proven for human user management.
2. **Blast Radius**: Prompt injection impact scales with agent tool access. Minimize tool inventory and enforce deterministic (not inferred) permissions.
3. **Defense Layers**: Data trustworthiness, identity/access control, runtime behavior monitoring, and human accountability are all required; no single layer suffices.
4. **Instruction Hierarchy**: Cannot be relied upon as a structural defense. Require deterministic permission enforcement independent of prompts.
5. **Human in the Loop**: Must be competent domain experts with accountability, not ceremonial approval. Non-repudiation and traceability essential for consequential actions.
6. **Observability**: Monitor agent behavior (tool invocations, data flows, C2 patterns), not just inputs. Trace entire attack chains across persistence mechanisms.
7. **Persistence Matters**: Agents maintaining state (heartbeats, memory, logs) are more dangerous when compromised; state machine design and cleanup critical.

talks.title: BlueHat 2026: Certificates in 2026: Alive, well, and shorter than ever
talks.teaser: Explores shrinking public certificate lifetimes and walks through ACME automation, CAA restrictions, and transparency log monitoring.
talks.summary:
Publicly trusted TLS certificates are on a mandated path toward much shorter lifetimes: stepping stones include a 200-day maximum in 2026, 100 days the following year, and 47 days by 2029 under CA/Browser Forum ballot SC081v3, with more frequent domain control validation. The speaker explains why browser vendors favor shorter validity as a practical substitute for weak real-world revocation, and why manual renewal cannot scale once renewals approach monthly cadence.

The middle of the session covers defender-oriented mechanics: the ACME protocol and its HTTP, DNS, and TLS-ALPN validation challenges, including risks when web servers receive broad DNS API credentials; CAA DNS records to block shadow or unauthorized issuance; and certificate transparency logs as a monitoring surface, illustrated with large-scale log analytics and readiness bucketing for upcoming validity limits.

The close walks through an MSRC-reported dangling DNS pattern against Azure App Service custom domains, where abandoned CNAME records plus predictable host naming enabled trusted certificate issuance on former customer subdomains at large scale, with CAA as a mitigating control and platform changes reducing default exposure. Practitioners are urged to automate renewal, enforce CAA, monitor transparency logs, and delete DNS when decommissioning cloud resources.

talks.title: BlueHat 2026: Agentic AI failure modes: A year in the field
talks.teaser: Updates a red team's taxonomy of agentic AI failure modes, with case studies of memory hijacking and approval bypass.
talks.summary:
Microsoft's AI red team revisits the taxonomy of failure modes for agentic AI that it published a year earlier. The speaker defines agents as autonomous software that can perceive and act within its surroundings, then explains which failure modes are new to agents and which are generative AI issues that agents amplify. The list has grown from 27 entries to 34.

New areas include supply chain risk in MCP servers, skill files and model choices, goal hijacking instead of whole-agent jailbreaks, weak trust between agents in multi-agent systems, computer-use attacks such as malicious ads on web pages, session context contamination, and MCP sampling. Three case studies followed. In the first, an outside attacker split a payload across emails that an assistant summarised, which led it to write to long-term memory, and the agent chose which approval step applied. In the second, aliased commands slipped past deterministic controls to read memory and post it to a website. In the third, a claimed accessibility need persuaded an agent to skip approval for sending email.

The practical advice is to make approval deterministic and outside the model's control, restrict which tools can write to memory, inventory MCP servers and skills, track the provenance of context so actions can be traced, and apply cryptographic trust between agents. The main point for red teams is to target the harness and architecture, since chaining small weaknesses around the model is often enough.

talks.title: BlueHat 2026: Double-edged AI: Securing the software supply chain in the autonomous era
talks.teaser: Traces recent supply chain attacks where AI-written code, AI-hunting malware and autonomous bots hit CI/CD pipelines.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a run of software supply chain attacks from the past year and the role AI played in each. It opens with the August 2025 compromise of the NX build tool. The malicious version searched developer machines and CI/CD runners for npm, GitHub and cloud credentials, and it also scanned for installed AI coding agents and ran them with safety features disabled to hunt for sensitive data. The workflow flaw it abused had come from an AI-generated pull request that an AI reviewer approved.

The middle section covers later incidents. Shai-Hulud was a self-replicating npm worm that used harvested credentials to infect more packages, compromising over 500 packages and leaking roughly 14,000 credentials into more than 20,000 public GitHub repositories. The speakers then describe a campaign by a group they call TeamPCP, which compromised Trivy, an LLM proxy framework and Checkmarx KICS, and which reportedly used Claude to help build its malware. HackerBot Claw, an autonomous agent running on Claude Opus 4.5, exploited misconfigured GitHub Actions workflows across seven open-source projects and achieved remote code execution in six. PRT Scan later followed a similar playbook in six waves, becoming language-aware by the last one.

The closing part covers defenses and practical lessons. AI code review and AI-driven package review can catch issues that scanners miss, and AI remediation shortens fix times. The practical advice includes human review of AI-generated CI/CD changes, separating the author and approver roles, guarding against hallucinated package names, requiring approval for first-time contributors, pinning dependencies to immutable references, monitoring CI runners and their network egress, and enforcing cooldown periods before adopting new package releases.

talks.title: BlueHat 2026: Pulling strings: From user to global admin via appIdUris
talks.teaser: Shows how a low-privilege Entra user reached global admin by abusing a loosely validated OAuth audience string.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at a part of OAuth that is often overlooked: the audience claim in access tokens and how Microsoft Entra handles application identifier URIs. By default, any user in a tenant can register an application, and a resource app can define its own roles that an administrator consents to. The speaker explains how these pieces fit together and why the audience tells a resource which service a token was issued for.

The research began with attempts to get around the verified-domain filter on identifier URIs, and that filter held up. Stepping back, the speaker noticed that the portal enforced URI formatting while the manifest accepted arbitrary strings. Comparing service principal names across tenants revealed that Azure AD Graph still accepted an old, non-URI identifier, microsoft.azure.activedirectory, which was unreserved in most tenants. By registering that string on a self-owned resource app, assigning it a role that allows role management, and requesting a token, a low-privilege user could add themselves to the global admin role.

Cameron Vincent from MSRC described the response. The case was triaged within minutes, and Microsoft stopped allowing arbitrary identifier strings by default, for both admins and non-admins. Developers were advised to validate the audience, tenant ID, subject, scope and roles claims, and to use the object ID rather than email or preferred username to identify users. The main takeaways are to keep accepted audiences in sync with what is reserved in Entra, and to return to a dead-end problem from a new angle.

talks.title: BlueHat 2026: When browsers become agents: The emerging security risks of AI-powered browsers
talks.teaser: Maps the threats facing AI-powered browsers, from prompt injection to malicious extensions, and how defenders can detect them.
talks.summary:
Dana Berriel, a principal security researcher at Microsoft Defender, describes agentic browsers as AI-enabled browsers that act for users, filling in forms, shopping, or sending email. She argues this is a current enterprise problem rather than a future one, citing a figure that 40% of enterprises already use them daily and that browsers host much of the workday. Because these browsers hold live sessions, tokens, cookies and passwords, they combine agent and browser risks in a new way.

She reviews the threat techniques: prompt injection, including web-hosted payloads, one of which deleted local files; credential and session theft; data exfiltration hidden in normal traffic; resource exhaustion that spends user tokens and GPUs; malicious extensions used for persistence; and unauthorized capture of screenshots, audio, files and clipboard data. A recorded demo showed an agent picking and installing a malicious extension from search results. Her analysis counted 57 threat families targeting AI browsers, 42 of them malicious.

The main case was a malicious extension that impersonated a legitimate one in a Chromium extension store, with good reviews, and reached over 900,000 users and 20,000 organizations. It scraped prompts, AI responses and URL history, re-enabled itself after being disabled, and sent the data to an attacker-controlled domain. Detection is hard because intent is difficult to separate from injected instructions and browsers lack standard logs. She introduced a contextual behavioral detection that flags suspicious AI browser actions, and closed by urging defenders to protect against both browser and agent techniques.

talks.title: BlueHat 2026: Securing the future of AI: Securing MCP with defense in depth patterns
talks.teaser: Shows MCP attack patterns such as rug pulls, DNS rebinding and tool shadowing, and layered gateway, registry and logging defenses.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at security risks in the Model Context Protocol, which has become a common integration layer between AI agents and external tools and data. The speaker explains that agent loops treat tool output as trusted, so anyone who controls what a tool returns can steer the agent. A demo of a rug pull showed a weather server that switched to a prompt injection after a set number of calls and leaked API keys without the user noticing.

Other cases covered DNS rebinding against a locally running MCP server, which can expose local services to a malicious web page, and tool hijacking and tool shadowing, where a malicious server pushes the model toward another server's tools. Since no single prompt filter or gateway stops all of these, the speaker argues for layered controls. A prototype gateway proxy inspected requests and responses and blocked the rug pull in the demo. The talk also recommends validating origin headers as the MCP specification describes and checking how far each SDK has been hardened.

For enterprises, the suggested pattern is an internal server registry, a central governed gateway, and role-based proxies that separate read tools from write tools, with every layer logging its decisions. The OWASP MCP top 10 is grouped into four control areas: identity, tools, context and visibility. The closing advice is to review each tool and input for whether it is trusted, allowed and safe to follow, and to threat-model MCP components like any other delegated authority.

talks.title: From access patterns to attack paths: Uncovering hidden cloud attack paths for end-to-end protection
talks.teaser: The presentation explains how mining sequential access logs exposes implicit cloud resource chains that static posture tools never map.
talks.summary:
Cloud posture products excel at configuration: IAM links, network rules, and infrastructure-as-code intent. They struggle when compromise spreads along paths that only appear in day-to-day usage, such as a workload that always reads a vault secret before touching storage. The speaker argues that gap leaves defenders unable to answer what else is at immediate risk when one resource is breached.

The proposed capability learns operational dependencies from normalized data-plane logs across services and tenants. It flags repeated temporal sequences where the same identity reaches one resource and then another within a short window, scores strength with an operational dependency ratio, and filters noise through long-horizon violation checks so high-confidence edges survive at petabyte scale. The result is a behavioral dependency graph that reflects how the environment actually runs, not only what policies allow.

For practitioners, the graph is meant to sharpen incident response by mapping blast radius and likely lateral movement, support hunting over chains that never appear in RBAC diagrams, and ground posture reviews in real interaction patterns. Retrospectives on major cloud breaches illustrate how known KMS, compute, and storage linkages could have narrowed containment if those implicit chains had been visible when alerts fired.

talks.title: INTERN(al) MSRC variant hunting: From multi-tenant authorization to MCP
talks.teaser: Walks through variant hunting on multi-tenant Entra apps and MCP OAuth consent flows, with fixes for each class.
talks.summary:
The talk comes from Microsoft's Vulnerabilities and Mitigations team, which validates reports, checks fixes and runs variant hunts. The first part covers multi-tenant sign-in. The speakers explain that roles, email and UPN claims cannot be trusted across tenants, that object IDs should be used instead, and that an attacker can swap the tenant in the authorization URL for common to reach an app meant for one organization.

To check about 6,000 internal multi-tenant apps, the team built an automated tool called Impostor. It signed in from outside tenants, granted itself every role it could, and flagged successful callbacks for human review. Most flags were false positives, where the front end allowed login but the back end denied API calls. Real findings included an internal chatbot that exposed incident data from ICM and a Copilot feature whose bot token was issued without any authentication.

The second part covers Model Context Protocol servers. A Word online MCP server needed no authentication and let callers run queries on production logs. In Azure MCP samples, XSS and CSRF flaws in the consent flow allowed auto-approval, and the OAuth state was not checked against consent, so a victim's code could reach an attacker. The fix adds a host-controlled consent cookie, and the MCP best practices were updated. Takeaways: make apps single tenant or allow-list tenant IDs, authenticate every endpoint, and treat samples as code that needs review.

talks.title: BlueHat Asia: Exploiting the pipeline: Real-world CI/CD vulnerabilities and how to secure them
talks.teaser: Covers common CI/CD pipeline misconfigurations that let attackers run code or steal secrets, plus how to fix them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with CI/CD basics: pipelines that build, test and deploy code, usually with access to secrets. It separates direct poisoned pipeline execution, where an attacker edits a workflow through a pull request, from indirect attacks that tamper with a dependency the workflow uses. GitHub Actions serves as the main example.

Each misconfiguration comes with a case. A privileged trigger that checks out untrusted pull request code can leak secrets. Untrusted values such as branch names, titles or comments injected into run commands allow code execution, and passing them through environment variables is the safer pattern. Artifacts from a low-trust workflow can overwrite trusted files downstream, and a persistent self-hosted runner tied to a public repository can be backdoored by outside contributors. A workflow_run chain can pass untrusted input to a higher-privilege job, and checking out a branch name instead of a commit SHA leaves a gap between approval and execution. An approval check that looks at the wrong actor let a Dependabot-driven change slip through auto-merge.

Brief notes cover Azure DevOps, CircleCI and AWS CodeBuild settings that can expose secrets to fork pull requests. The closing advice: pin commit SHAs, use ephemeral runners, limit token permissions, sanitize inputs, require multiple reviewers and commit signing, and avoid untrusted third-party orbs.

talks.title: BlueHat Asia: Augmented disruption using graph-based scoring
talks.teaser: Shows how attack graphs and contextual asset risk scores enable early augmented disruption against business email compromise.
talks.summary:
The session contrasts reactive alerting with a proactive model likened to smart sprinklers versus fire alarms, arguing that traditional detections often fire only after attackers are already inside and lateral movement or exfiltration has begun. It introduces augmented disruption: combining an attack graph that fuses progression, victim profiling, and cross-source correlation with a contextual asset risk score that turns faint early signals into quantitative decisions about when and how hard to intervene.

Using business email compromise as the main thread, the speakers outline vendor-chain risk, payroll and conversation-hijack variants beyond inbox rules, and role-dependent attack paths—for example billing administrators versus Exchange administrators. Graph-backed scenarios show why isolating the wrong user fails when the real target sits elsewhere, such as credential paths through devices to a critical account. The contextual score blends blast radius, critical assets, threat-actor profile match, and progression context to justify soft actions like user suspension hours or a day before conventional BEC confidence peaks.

Operational walkthroughs cover HR consent-abuse and accounts-payable conversation hijack timelines, plus early endpoint cases tied to ransomware progression. Reported outcomes include intercepting roughly twenty-five net-new attacks daily near token use, near-zero false positives on next-move prediction, and on the order of five hundred remediation hours saved. Takeaways stress early intervention, exposure-aware monitoring, and context-specific disruptive actions rather than one-size-fits-all containment.

talks.title: BlueHat Asia keynote: Inside the underground: A deep dive into new initial access techniques
talks.teaser: Explores indirect initial access paths through vendors, dev tooling, and logistics partners instead of direct endpoint compromise.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that defenders and attackers both win or lose on paths beside the main application. A formative shared-hosting engagement showed that abusing a provider’s support portal to reset SSH credentials could yield full server access without touching the customer web app. That mindset became “3D security”: libraries, runtimes, frameworks, and adjacent services—not only the visible product—form one attack surface, echoed in years of image-library research and stacked skills that later fed other projects.

The middle of the talk pairs demonstration-grade cable-TV work with modern initial-access cases. It describes tapping distribution links, altering transport-stream scrambling indicators so injected feeds appear legitimate to setup boxes, and remotely crashing receivers. It then walks through supply-chain style breaches: a leaked container image with cloud API keys used to push scripts through developer IDEs that exfiltrated environment secrets from thousands of organizations, and Jenkins compromises at software vendors that unlocked Git repositories, client code, and hardcoded keys affecting hundreds of enterprises linked to high-profile ransomware activity.

Practitioners should inventory third parties, SaaS, CI systems, and physical logistics software as first-class entry points alongside corporate endpoints. Cases such as cash-management vendors for ATMs and airline crew pickup scheduling show how small operational apps can delay flights or disrupt cash networks. The close warns that API-linked supply chains and emerging agent layers will multiply these graphs, so protection must trace the same indirect routes attackers already use.

talks.title: BlueHat Asia: When servers get phished: OAuth token misbinding and server-side CSRF in social logins
talks.teaser: Explains OAuth state flaws in social logins and integrations that let attackers capture victims' authorization codes.
talks.summary:
The talk covers social OAuth, meaning the "login with" buttons and third-party integrations such as calendar or cloud-drive connections found on many sites. It starts with the authorization code flow and the parameters that shape it. The identity provider fixes the redirect URI and scope, so the presenter focuses on the state value, arguing that it does more than guard against CSRF.

Four classes of flaw follow, each illustrated with previously reported and fixed Microsoft issues. The first is server-side CSRF and token misbinding: a genuine consent link carrying the attacker's state value gets the victim's authorization code stored in the attacker's account. If the identity provider remembers the app and skips consent, this becomes one-click takeover. The second class is state-driven routing in SaaS subdomains, where the redirect target is taken from data inside state. One case had no domain validation, another used a URL fragment to truncate the host, and a third only checked that the top-level domain had four letters. The third class is missing or misused state, where a connection completes without any token, so an attacker can link their own third-party account to a victim. The fourth is CSRF protection present on the first return but absent from a later redirect that carries the token after code exchange.

The impact was generally rated high rather than critical because a victim still has to click a link, though the stolen codes could carry broad rights such as read and write access to a victim's Google Drive. For practitioners, the takeaway is to bind state to the user's session, check it on every redirect including those after code exchange, and not assume a consent page is safe because its URL looks legitimate.

talks.title: BlueHat Asia: Hack the context: MCP VULNfest
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning BlueHat Asia: Hack the context: MCP VULNfest.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this BlueHat Asia presentation, security researcher Vishal Chan (IIT Bombay) and Nikhil (head of PE Security) explore the attack surface of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and AI assistant integrations. The speakers explain the architecture of MCP—connecting AI models, context, and external tools/servers—and demonstrate how adversaries can bend context rather than traditional application code. They disclose an attack chain weaponizing a popular AI assistant's code interpreter into an unauthorized Command and Control (C2) agent, and outline security frameworks and mitigations across enterprise, developer, and end-user layers.

### Key Topics
- **MCP Architecture & Adoption**: MCP acts as a standardized two-way protocol connecting MCP hosts (AI applications), clients (interfaces/connectors), and servers (tools or data sources such as databases, file systems, Slack, and GitHub). Backed by major players like Anthropic, Microsoft, and OpenAI, it supersedes one-way plugins and static RAG implementations.
- **MCP Attack Matrix & Attack Vectors**: Key threats include prompt injection, tool poisoning (embedding hidden malicious instructions or metadata in tool descriptions visible to the LLM but hidden in the UI), data exfiltration (API keys, credentials, conversation histories), rugpull attacks (trusted tools silently updating server-side capabilities without reapproval), and authentication/supply chain risks.
- **Real-World Vulnerability Classes**: The talk notes real-world examples such as MCP remote RCE, an Anthropic MCP Inspector debug tool meant for local troubleshooting that was reachable from the public internet, file system server escapes, and preference manipulation.
- **Universal Attack Chain (AI Assistant to C2)**: Nikhil details an exploit chain turning a top commercial AI assistant into an adversary C2 agent by exploiting its code interpreter through extensive prompt engineering, sandbox privilege escalation, and network egress bypass.

### Technical Details
- **The Red Towel Problem (Willpower Depletion)**: Vishal describes an incident building an MCP server for memory forensics on 25 samples. Repeated authorization prompts (depletion of willpower) caused him to blindly approve requests after eight popups, resulting in the model dumping and executing a malicious process on the host machine.
- **C2 Exploitation Walkthrough**:
  - *Phase 1 (Code Execution)*: After 8–10 hours of prompt engineering to understand and bypass guardrails, the researchers achieved execution of `/bin/bash` and verified write capability by creating a file in `/tmp`.
  - *Phase 2 (Privilege Escalation)*: The sandbox execution user was present in the Linux `sudo` list, allowing privilege escalation to `root` and reading protected files like `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/hosts`.
  - *Phase 3 (Egress & C2 Establishment)*: To ensure results were not AI hallucinations, the team tested outbound callbacks. While port 443 and other standard ports were heavily monitored and blocked, outbound traffic on port 80 was permitted. HTTP `POST`, `HEAD`, and `OPTIONS` verbs were blocked by firewall filtering, but HTTP `GET` requests were allowed. The team spun up a VPS and polled commands via HTTP GET, executing them on the AI provider's infrastructure as root and returning command outputs.

### Takeaways
- **MCP Gateways & Registries**: Deploying an MCP gateway (such as IBM's MCP Context Forge or Docker's sandboxed gateway) provides essential governance, access policies (e.g., allowing read/comment on GitHub while denying push/merge/branch operations), and audit logging. MCP registries act as vetted app stores.
- **Layered Defense Framework**:
  - *Enterprise*: Runtime isolation via lightweight VMs, strict network egress controls, and continuous AI red teaming.
  - *Developer*: Strict input/output sanitization, static/dynamic analysis (SAST/DAST), dependency checking, secret management, and assuming all tool descriptions are untrusted input.
  - *Process Isolation*: Utilizing Linux kernel isolation primitives such as `seccomp` and AppArmor to enforce per-process execution boundaries.
  - *User*: Limiting tool connections to verified registries, rate limiting, and awareness against notification fatigue.

talks.title: BlueHat Asia keynote: Where the mind is without fear: Building a secure, AI-powered world
talks.teaser: Argues that AI systems need threat modeling from hardware up, covering prompt injection, memory poisoning and weak randomness.
talks.summary:
This BlueHat Asia keynote argues that AI-powered systems should be built on sound architecture and a people-first mindset. The speaker compares design principles from classical and modern architecture to layers in software, arguing that simple, well-separated designs are easier to defend. Users should be counted beyond the person at the screen, including family members and bystanders, when modeling threats.

The middle of the talk treats threat modeling as a structured practice. It covers documenting product requirements, identity and data flows, and mapping each threat to a matching mitigation, then recording residual risk. For AI stacks, the speaker notes that probabilistic model layers cannot be guaranteed to behave deterministically. Prompt injection hidden in an email or shared document is shown as a way to make an assistant leak private data, and memory poisoning is described as a persistent threat to AI memory. Suggested defenses include input and output checks, separating code from data, validating memory content, and avoiding alert fatigue from constant user prompts. Logging that preserves causal chains of events is also urged.

The closing section urges deeper reasoning over shallow checklists, using historical examples of overlooked discoveries and questioned assumptions. Weak random number generators and training data that underrepresents some groups are presented as failures that can break guarantees or produce unfair outcomes. The takeaway is to understand how a model was built, threat model early, and innovate responsibly.

talks.title: BlueHat Asia: From anti-patterns to assurance: Unleashing the power of variant hunting
talks.teaser: Outlines variant hunting for security anti-patterns, from bearer token leak analysis through the Apex assurance framework.
talks.summary:
The session begins with a counterfeiting investigation in which one nearly perfect bill exposed many related forgeries, using that story to argue that one software flaw can reveal families of related weaknesses. The presenters define variant hunting as searching for recurring security anti-patterns across code and configuration, and they contrast it with threat hunting, penetration testing, and narrow threat modeling reviews.

They walk through a bearer token leak in the Azure portal where a crafted portal link triggers client-side JavaScript to send authenticated requests bearing stolen tokens to an attacker-controlled host. Contributing-causes analysis covers untrusted page parameters and unsafe URL construction; pattern extraction generalizes the issue into client-side URL injection spanning page parameters, query strings, and partial hostname injection. Their Apex model structures lifecycle work from exploration and risk reduction through durable mitigation and continuous assurance.

On the token-leak pattern they combined parameter review, dynamic scanning, and CodeQL to find instances, drove spot fixes and longer-term portal SDK and central blocking controls, and added scanners and telemetry to catch regressions. They briefly tie similar thinking to unauthenticated Azure functions and metrics such as injection rate to prioritize leadership action. Closing guidance emphasizes root causes, cross-service patterns, repeatable frameworks, and measurable risk.

talks.title: BlueHat Asia: Cross-tenant RCEs at scale: Breaking Azure and getting caught
talks.teaser: Traces how argument injection in Azure integration runtimes led to cross-tenant code execution in Purview and Synapse.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through research into Microsoft Purview and Azure Synapse Analytics, looking for a way that a customer's scan could reach code running on shared Azure integration runtimes. The speaker explains how the self-hosted integration runtime, a Java and .NET component that connects to data sources, can be downloaded and studied locally, and how its launch arguments are assembled from connection properties such as a MongoDB server name entered in the interface.

The core finding is an argument injection. The Java launcher takes its executable path and parameters from user-controlled settings, so the speaker could make it start PowerShell and use a comment marker so that everything after the injected command was ignored. The payload worked on a self-hosted runtime. By changing the runtime type in a proxy, the speaker showed that a shared Azure runtime accepted the same request, which the speaker argued would let an attacker read other tenants' credentials and process memory. For Synapse, a regular expression filter that blocked a Snowflake file-download command was bypassed by inserting an SQL comment. That gave a route to drop a DLL into a directory the runtime loads dynamically. Once the DLL ran, many processes across the region sent requests back, which drew contact from Microsoft's response team.

The talk closes with lessons for practitioners: no environment is as secure as it looks, and shared runtimes, permissions and isolation deserve close review. The speaker also describes reporting mistakes, including duplicate tagging of a batch of submissions and a lost bounty when a submission was blocked, and encourages researchers to follow a lead through to the end.

talks.title: BlueHat Asia: From alert to disruption: Evidence-driven risk assessment for OAuth cloud applications
talks.teaser: Explains how AI agents gather evidence from scattered cloud logs to score OAuth apps as true or false positives.
talks.summary:
OAuth cloud applications are a common entry point in cloud environments. A user who clicks through a malicious consent screen can grant an app tokens that read mail, send messages or download files. Legitimate and malicious apps often show the same consent experience, so a SOC analyst receiving an alert has to join application metadata, sign-in and consent logs, and API activity across separate tables before deciding whether the app is a threat. This manual pivoting is slow and easily confuses analysts working through a queue of alerts.

The talk presents a multi-agent design that automates this triage. An orchestration agent takes a natural-language request or an alert ID and calls a lookup tool that returns the application ID, tenant, alert description and timestamp. A planner then chooses which analyzers to run. Analyzers look at metadata for brand impersonation and app age, sign-in behaviour, API activity, and dormancy before suddenly becoming active. An evidence report correlates their findings. A panel of expert personas, including statistical, forensic, email and consent-phishing experts, is drawn from a retrieved attack-pattern knowledge base and returns a verdict with a confidence score and a disruption recommendation.

A demo case showed an app with a lookalike name, using a zero in place of the letter O, and a reply URL with a swapped character. It had been created only days earlier, held mail read and send permissions, and recorded heavy mail and attachment reads plus many created message rules. It was classified as a true positive. On a benchmark of more than a thousand real-world samples, the system reported 95% precision and 72% recall, with precision prioritised so benign business apps are not disrupted. Planned work includes an evidence graph linking indicators, automatic enrichment of the knowledge base, and wider data coverage to reduce missed threats, aiming to move from reactive detection to proactive disruption.

talks.title: BlueHat Asia 2025: Hotfix without the fix: Runtime security with "Shimit"
talks.teaser: Shows how shim-based runtime interception blocks vulnerable Linux library calls when official patches are missing or delayed.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a recurring operational problem: organizations remain exposed between vulnerability disclosure and patch deployment, even when vendors ship fixes promptly. The Equifax Apache Struts incident illustrates how delayed rollout can still lead to massive data loss despite an available patch.

The proposed approach, called Shimit, uses symbol overloading and LD_PRELOAD to insert shim shared libraries ahead of real implementations. Intercepted calls can be blocked or validated before optionally delegating to the original symbol via dlsym. A toy getpid demo fakes a process ID to show load order; a CVE-2024-2961 example targets iconv conversions from UTF-8 to ISO-2022-CN-EXT, blocking the dangerous path that otherwise produces a one-byte buffer overflow.

Practitioners learn a stopgap mitigation that avoids recompiling legacy applications, but only when vulnerable functions are dynamically linked and resolvable symbols exist. Static linking, inlining, or absent symbols fall outside scope, yet many widespread library flaws fit the model as bring-your-own runtime remediation.

talks.title: Security Chats: Defending Agentic AI with Deterministic Guardrails
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Security Chats: Defending Agentic AI with Deterministic Guardrails.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this installment of Microsoft Security Response Center's *Security Chats*, host Joe Miller speaks with Santiago Zanella, a principal researcher in AI security and privacy at Azure Research. The discussion centers on the security challenges emerging from increasingly autonomous and agentic AI systems, the inherent limitations of probabilistic defenses (such as secondary classifier models), and ongoing research into deterministic guardrails, specifically using information flow control and the Dual LLM architecture.

### Key Topics
- **Transition to Agentic Autonomy:** As LLMs gain agency, tool execution capabilities, and browser or computer-use interfaces, they are entrusted with confidential data and credentials. Operating without robust controls risks severe prompt injection and data exfiltration issues.
- **Offense vs. Defense Balance:** Santiago highlights that utility currently outpaces security across the industry, giving attackers an advantage. However, AI may eventually provide defenders with a net security gain in the long term through proactive attack surface exploration.
- **Failure of Probabilistic Mitigations:** Relying solely on probabilistic AI classifiers or layered model prompts provides only a first-line filter against unsophisticated attacks. Motivated attackers consistently bypass these soft layers, necessitating deterministic, traditional software engineering boundaries.

### Technical Details
- **Dual LLM Architecture & Information Flow Control:** Because transformer architectures inherently blend instructions and untrusted data into a single channel, full separation inside the model is fundamentally impossible without severely crippling utility. Building upon Simon Willison’s Dual LLM design pattern—which separates a privileged planning LLM from a quarantined LLM handling untrusted data—Santiago's team incorporates information flow control. Data ingested from outside tools is tainted with labels (such as 'untrusted') that propagate across contexts. High-stakes actions (e.g., banking transactions, external emails) are governed by deterministic security policies that prohibit execution when context contains untrusted or tainted data.
- **Variable Passing & Performance:** Rather than injecting raw tool outputs into the planner context, variable passing stores tool results in orchestrator memory and passes references. While current multi-LLM architectures see an approximate 3x token usage expansion, Santiago projects optimizations can bring overhead down toward 10%.
- **Key Vulnerabilities and Research Tools:** 
  - *Embedding Inversion:* Techniques like 'vec2text' demonstrate that high-dimensional semantic embeddings can be inverted to reconstruct original text verbatim, requiring embeddings to receive the same confidentiality safeguards as raw data.
  - *Optimization-Based Attacks:* Tools like GCG (greedy coordinate gradient) allow prompt optimization on open-weights models to transfer successfully against proprietary models.
  - *Security Platforms & Frameworks:* Mentioned testing tools and benchmarks include PyRIT, the UK AI Security Institute's Inspect AI, Gray Swan Arena, Lakera's Gandalf challenges, and MSRC's LLMail Inject competition.

### Takeaways
- **Deterministic Harnesses over More AI:** The belief that prompt injection can be cured by 'throwing more AI at the problem' is a critical misconception. Reliable protection requires treating LLMs as stochastic black boxes encapsulated within deterministic harnesses.
- **Ecosystem Advice:** Security researchers of all skill levels are encouraged to explore AI security through hands-on CTFs, bug programs (such as Zero Day Quest), and community resources, analyzing the fragile assumptions built into emerging autonomous systems.

talks.title: Security Chats: AI Security in Practice: Copilot, AEBA, and the Next Big Risks
talks.teaser: A Microsoft AI security leader outlines emerging AI risks like prompt injection and how security teams should build skills.
talks.summary:
Pushkar Saraf, director of security at Microsoft AI, discusses how securing AI products differs from traditional software. He argues that existing controls still apply, but AI systems gather information across many sources, and a single prompt can steer an LLM toward unintended actions. He proposes AI entity behavior analytics, which he prefers to UEBA, as a way to watch what agents access and do.

On balancing speed and security, he says products should be secure by default, yet industry-wide vulnerabilities still demand fast mitigations because agents used by millions amplify impact. He expects governments to set data residency and privacy rules and sees supply chain risk growing as agents embed in daily tools. He points to the industry top 10 list of LLM risks as a baseline, highlighting excessive agency, least privilege and anomalous agent access. For the coming year he expects prompt injection to dominate, with output handling and training data poisoning beneath it.

For smaller organizations without a dedicated security team, he suggests relying on established industry practices, external vetting and contract-based expertise, then building in-house depth as the business grows. On hiring, he values curiosity, an understanding of system design such as model context protocol, and hands-on practice over theory. He also says his team is building AI agents to speed up threat analysis.

talks.title: From GitHub to gatherings: Roberto's journey through tech & friendship
talks.teaser: A summit-floor interview covers agentic security operations, open-source learning, and how relationships shape a research career.
talks.summary:
Hosts speak with a former Microsoft security researcher who now leads work on applying artificial intelligence to security operations for a media organization. He describes teaching a multi-day class alongside his full brother, focused on end-to-end design, evaluation, and operational wrapping of AI agents for large-scale environments.

When asked what most shaped his career, he emphasizes people met inside and outside the company, and advises finding peers by following personal passion and breaking the ice despite shyness. He learns by dissecting open-source projects, sometimes reimplementing ideas, and watching technical presentations. He contrasts broad AI with agentic systems that use large language models to reason, decide, and act, noting that protecting them feels familiar from an engineering standpoint while novel artifacts and autonomous actions raise new concerns.

He recounts building agent frameworks on top of a Microsoft-originated Dapper project, first under a Floki-inspired name and later as Dapper Agents, with stickers and an upcoming presentation. He points listeners to his Cyber WarDog social handles for training follow-ups and open-source work, and closes by prioritizing friends and community on the conference floor over chasing every session.

talks.teaser: Researchers learn how to coordinate with Microsoft’s security response center before conference talks, blogs, or other public disclosure.
talks.summary:
The session centers on responsible disclosure when findings touch Microsoft products. Presenters describe giving the vendor advance notice before a conference talk, sharing slides, explaining timelines and research angle, and waiting for approval so feedback can improve accuracy and tone.

Coordinated vulnerability disclosure is treated as non‑negotiable: nothing unfixed should be published, even when bounty disputes run hot. For planned write‑ups or talks on resolved issues, they recommend emailing MSRC, supplying draft material, and working with a case manager through complex fixes—especially in cloud stacks where many internal teams must align.

Practical takeaways include reading Microsoft’s disclosure policy, asking when rules feel ambiguous, testing only on owned on‑prem systems or within published cloud and black‑box guidelines, and avoiding out‑of‑scope targets. Patience and steady communication with MSRC are emphasized as the norm for long-running cases.

talks.teaser: Non-financial MSRC recognition, leaderboards, and events deliver career paths for vulnerability researchers beyond bug bounties.
talks.summary:
Microsoft’s Security Response Center describes incentive programs that sit alongside paid bug bounties. Non-financial recognition is positioned as career capital: quarterly leaderboards, an annual most valuable researcher ranking, and linked events can still change hiring prospects and future income even when no award check arrives.

The talk walks through recognition parties at Black Hat and Blue Hat, invitations for on-site collaboration and conference talks, podcast and blog spotlights, and ongoing expansion of those formats. A newer researcher resource center is highlighted for onboarding guidance, curated training links, peer learning, and clearer visibility into how MSRC engagement works.

Researchers recount leaderboard placement and community events as validation that drew respect from peers, conference introductions, speaking opportunities at Blue Hat, and follow-on work. The practical takeaway is to treat ranking points, spotlights, and MSRC-hosted forums as deliberate paths for reputation, networking, and jobs—not only as side effects of bounty payouts.

talks.title: Tips and advice from MSRC security researchers
talks.teaser: Shares practical advice on persistence, note-taking, collaboration and learning resources for bug bounty research.
talks.summary:
The talk gathers advice from security researchers who report bugs to Microsoft's bounty programs. The first theme is persistence. Researchers are urged to accept failure as part of the work, since many people give up before they get results, and to try unusual approaches that others may have skipped. Keeping detailed notes is another recommendation, because a bug that cannot be triggered today may become exploitable after nearby code is patched and the notes allow it to be revisited.

The speakers suggest starting with software already used day to day, which shortens setup and helps keep motivation up. They also describe research as a hypothesis-driven method: form a hypothesis, build an environment, test it and record the result. One researcher keeps network captures, backups and service logs to compare how a product looked at different points in time and to spot newly added features. Collaborating with other researchers and attending conferences are presented as useful ways to get support.

For learning, the speakers point to publicly disclosed reports, researcher blogs with write-ups, bug bounty platform reports, books on web application hacking, and training labs such as Hack The Box. The closing message is to start, stay with the work, and learn from how others solved and disclosed their bugs.

talks.title: Zero Day Quest training: Access denied? Exploiting common access control pitfalls
talks.teaser: Covers common access control flaws, from missing authorization checks to OAuth misconfigurations, plus a hands-on CTF.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a crash course on access control, which the speaker splits into authentication, authorization and accountability. Failures are described as specification mistakes, such as risky default permissions, or enforcement gaps, where a low-privilege user can still reach a sensitive endpoint. Broken access control tops the OWASP Top 10 from 2021, and MSRC severity depends on how sensitive the exposed data is and what an attacker needs beforehand.

Bug patterns come next. Missing authorization checks can be surfaced by feeding an OpenAPI specification and a token into an open-source tool that flags endpoints answering 200 where a 401 belongs. For insecure direct object references, sequential IDs are easy to iterate, and hard-to-guess identifiers still count unless they are explicitly secret. Path reversal is shown alongside encoding and sanitizer bypasses, including double encoding, nested sequences, null bytes and Unicode. Client-side restrictions appear in editable cookies and response codes, and default-off feature flags may expose untested behaviour. OAuth pitfalls include leaked client secrets, implicit-flow tokens exposed through redirects and logs, missing state parameters enabling CSRF, overly broad scopes, and OAuth used for login without OpenID Connect.

The talk ends with a hands-on capture-the-flag of five challenges and four flags, run from a Docker container. The first IDOR challenge is solved by iterating order IDs in Burp Intruder and spotting the one response with a different length. The main takeaway is to use two accounts and swap identifiers to prove real impact.

talks.title: Security Research in Copilot Studio
talks.teaser: Maps Copilot Studio's architecture and Power Platform integrations to show where security bugs hide and how to report them.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) virtual session, Security Program Manager Alyssa Str introduces Scott Gorick, Principal Security Architect for Power Platform and Dynamics. Gorick outlines the architecture of Microsoft Copilot Studio, details how it fits within the broader Power Platform and Microsoft Entra ecosystems, and provides guidance for external security researchers conducting vulnerability research and submitting high-efficacy bug reports to MSRC bounty programs.

### Key Topics
- **Trust Boundaries and Identity Plane**: Gorick explains that Microsoft Entra ID forms the identity plane and the primary trust boundary. The highest-tier bounty targets involve cross-tenant information disclosure, followed by environment-level boundary escapes, resource permissions, and data loss prevention (DLP) bypasses. Dataverse also implements its own distinct authorization model.
- **Copilot Studio and Power Platform Composition**: The platform enables low-code/no-code, pro-code, and agentic workflows. Copilot Studio integrates tightly with over 1,000 pre-built connectors, Power Automate flows, Power Apps, Power Pages, Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Builder, and Azure Bot Service. Gorick demonstrates dynamic chaining, generative answers over public or uploaded data, and tracing mode for inspecting model decision-making.
- **Platform Vulnerability vs. Developer Misconfiguration**: A core message is distinguishing between developer misconfigurations (e.g., publishing an unauthenticated bot with SharePoint access or testing as a tenant Global Admin who has default break-glass access) and legitimate platform vulnerabilities (e.g., bypassing configured DLP policies, security feature bypasses, IDOR, or SSRF).

### Technical Details
- **Vulnerability Surfaces**: Key areas for security testing include Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) when copilot fetches URLs for grounding, Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) on admin/API endpoints, indirect prompt injection via conversational state stores or Dataverse, and file parsing/abuse from document uploads.
- **Connector and Identity Abuse**: Referring to external research by Samsung regarding OAuth application consent abuse for zero-click phishing, Gorick highlights how connectors can be abused for identity risks, aligning with OWASP low-code/no-code top risks.
- **Power Fx and Extensibility**: Power Fx acts as an expression language executing on nodes within agent flows or within Dataverse to concatenate strings and compose context. Pro-developer extensibility through Dataverse plugins and custom connectors provides critical attack surface often leveraged by top bug bounty researchers.
- **Governance and Administration**: Central administration is performed via the Power Platform Admin Center (PPAC) and managed environments. Gorick notes that tools like the Center of Excellence (CoE) Starter Kit highlight the governance controls and milestones researchers should investigate when looking for bypasses.

### Takeaways
Researchers should understand how Copilot Studio composes underlying infrastructure (Azure OpenAI, Azure Bot Service, Dataverse) and focus on platform-level boundary violations rather than standard configuration choices. Staying within the Bounty Rules of Engagement, testing with low-privilege accounts rather than Global Admins, and understanding what assumptions the application makes are crucial steps for identifying significant zero-day vulnerabilities.

talks.title: Zero Day Quest: Microsoft's Bug Bounty Program and AI Research
talks.teaser: Explains Microsoft's AI bug bar and bounty program, covering prompt injection, model poisoning and inferential disclosure categories.
talks.summary:
The session, part of Microsoft's Zero Day Quest research challenge, introduces the Microsoft Security Response Center's AI bug bounty program. Rewards for the Copilot scope have been doubled, with top awards now reaching $30,000. Only reports rated important or critical under the AI bug bar qualify for a payout.

The AI bug bar extends the existing Windows and online services bars with categories for AI systems. Inference manipulation includes prompt injection and input perturbation, model manipulation covers model and data poisoning, and inferential information disclosure covers training data reconstruction, membership and attribute inference, model stealing and input extraction. Severity rises with security impact and falls when the victim must take action. A hidden-text web page example shows how injected instructions can reach Copilot, and a later case used rendered image tags to exfiltrate data to an attacker server. Two lessons were highlighted: prompt injection must show a concrete security impact, and system prompt extraction is no longer in scope.

For newcomers, the speakers recommended hands-on challenges, conference recordings, research papers and other researchers' write-ups. Strong reports include the exact product URL, configuration choices, prompt text, evidence of the behaviour, and how often it reproduces. Reports are submitted through the researcher portal, where additional findings can be added later.

talks.title: Zero Day Quest - Learn to Red Team AI Systems Using PyRIT. Recorded December 2nd 2024
talks.teaser: Shows how the open-source PyRIT tool helps researchers find prompt-injection bugs that qualify for Microsoft's AI bounty.
talks.summary:
This session, presented by Microsoft Security Response Center staff, explains how Microsoft's AI bug bounty rewards reports of generative AI flaws. The presenters outline the AI bug bar, which groups issues into inference manipulation, model manipulation and inferential information disclosure, and stress that a qualifying bug must affect users beyond the researcher. They also cover rules of engagement: test only accounts you control, avoid denial-of-service, respect rate limits, and report through the researcher portal.

Rich Lundeen then introduces PyRIT, an open-source red teaming tool built by Microsoft's AI red team. He explains its building blocks: orchestrators that drive attack logic, prompt datasets, converters that transform prompts (such as Base64 encoding, translation or rendering text into an image), targets such as a chat model or a document store, and scorers that judge responses. A multi-turn demo shows a Crescendo-style attack using emoji-converted prompts. He stresses that the tool is best at getting past prompt-level mitigations rather than devising the exploit scenario.

An email assistant scenario shows how converters and orchestrators can be stacked: jailbreak templates delivered as message attachments, images carrying text, and translated or rap-battle phrasing. Martin Pouliot and Rich close with practical advice: understand the application's trust boundaries, look for places where untrusted input reaches a model that drives security-relevant actions, and submit reports with clear impact and reproduction steps.

talks.title: Submitting to MSRC: An Introduction to Submitting Security Research Findings
talks.teaser: Explains how to submit vulnerability findings to Microsoft's response team, follow case stages, and write reports that resolve faster.
talks.summary:
The talk walks researchers through submitting vulnerability findings to the Microsoft Security Response Center. It covers the kinds of reports accepted beyond software flaws, such as malicious activity hosted on Microsoft domains or IP ranges and abused apps. A submission first passes a review step, where staff decide whether there is enough detail to open a case. An accepted case then moves through reproduction, development and pre-release stages before it is marked complete. Timing depends on factors such as version currency, active exploitation and severity.

The talk then describes what makes a report high quality: accurate product and version details, the vulnerability class, potential impact, reproduction environment and steps, a working proof of concept, sound analysis, and optional remediation advice. Using the portal instead of email or social media, and answering requests within 72 hours, are presented as ways to shorten resolution. Bounty eligibility depends on potential impact, and out-of-scope items include unsupported versions and third-party add-ons. Researchers are warned not to access customer or Microsoft data.

Closing sections cover coordinated disclosure, including a 30-day window after a fix is published before details become public, and Safe Harbor protections for good-faith violations of the Rules of Engagement. Recognition comes through acknowledgements and leaderboard points. The main takeaway is to write complete reports, communicate through the portal, respect the disclosure timeline, and expect the develop and pre-release stages to take the longest.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S08: "It's By Design!"
talks.teaser: A veteran bounty hunter explains Microsoft by-design responses and lessons from real bounty disputes.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames how Microsoft Security Response Center classifies submissions as “by design,” out of scope, or ineligible for bounty, and why that label frustrates researchers who invested heavy effort. It walks through several cloud identity and productivity cases: Entra ID autologon abuse for enumeration and password guessing with weak logging, Exchange Online direct send for spoofed internal mail, anonymous listing of access packages that exposed administrator identities, Entra Connect misuse of cloud anchors to alter cloud-only accounts including privileged roles, and SharePoint migration APIs that let team owners forge file metadata without audit events—later extended to injected script on pages.

Outcomes varied. Some reports stayed closed or were dismissed until blogs or persistence forced reassessment; others earned large bounties after documentation-backed pushback or follow-on reports when mitigations failed. One Exchange remote PowerShell MFA bypass proved to be a mistaken test window after misreading how long policy changes take.

Closing guidance splits between vendors and finders: avoid automatic closures without dialogue, inconsistent answers, or employer pressure when a case is declined; keep researchers informed and ask them to validate fixes. Researchers are urged to read responses carefully, cite official docs, stay persistent, file separate reports for incomplete fixes, and verify conditions before submitting.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S05: Octo Tempest: A Year of Response
talks.teaser: Traces the Octo Tempest group's shift from SIM swapping to ransomware, and the social engineering and identity tactics behind it.
talks.summary:
Octo Tempest, a financially motivated group also tracked as Scattered Spider or Octopus, began around 2022 with SIM swapping and cryptocurrency theft against telecoms and crypto firms. By 2023 it had shifted toward data theft, extortion and ransomware, hitting large IT, retail, hospitality and entertainment organizations. The speakers describe its members as English-speaking people from Western countries, part of a wider online community called The Com. Initial access usually starts with lookalike domains, SMS phishing and fake login pages, plus impersonation of employees to help desks and pressure on overworked IT administrators.

Once inside, the group abuses tooling already present, such as EDR agents and enterprise software deployment platforms, to push its own credential stealers and persistence. It adds rogue federation providers to identity platforms, weakens conditional access rules, steals break-glass accounts and has joined incident response calls to read chats. Persistence hides among legitimate remote management tools and newly created virtual machines that mimic existing naming. Access can move from first foothold to global admin within 24 hours, and backup systems are also targeted.

The speakers recommend phishing-resistant MFA, compliant-device requirements that cover every location, and help desk procedures that refuse or escalate high-risk password and MFA resets. They urge least privilege and just-in-time access for EDR live response and deployment tools, blocking unapproved remote access software, and logging VM creation. Removing administrator privilege is a fast containment step, and incident teams should prepare out-of-band communications kept off corporate devices. They present the case as a pattern that similar criminal groups are likely to repeat.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S22: Security Content: Stop Flexing and Start Helping
talks.teaser: Explains why security content often fails non-experts and offers simple tests for writing clearer guidance.
talks.summary:
Sarah Young argues that security content is mostly written for other security specialists, who end up showing off rather than helping. She describes the "expert problem," where people who know a subject struggle to explain it, use acronyms without defining them, and copy the style of senior authors. She also points out that thought leadership often makes writing longer and harder to follow.

To test this, she manually reviewed about 200 pieces of security content, found through searches a newcomer would likely run, such as beginner fundamentals and how-to queries. Each item was scored out of six on criteria including whether it assumes no prior knowledge, gives steps one person can carry out, avoids sending readers to other resources, can be read in under an hour, and uses plain language. Vendor material made up about half the set and not-for-profit material about a third. Not-for-profit content scored best on accessibility, documentation scored better than podcasts, and vendor material scored lower. She also noted that three cloud providers' security best-practice documents each ran around 100 pages, which a busy administrator could not realistically work through.

Her remedy is to ask whether the reader can act on the content, whether it has a clear beginning, middle and end, and whether a non-specialist such as a parent or a frontline worker could follow it. She recommends plain language with acronyms explained, a short summary covering what, why and how, and brief cheat sheets for common tasks. She also urges authors to give definitive guidance, while being clear that security reduces risk rather than eliminating it, and to review existing material with colleagues.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S21: Building a Canarytoken to Monitor Windows Process Execution
talks.teaser: Shows how a registry-based trip wire alerts defenders when a chosen Windows program runs, with no agent installed.
talks.summary:
Casey Smith, from the Thinkst research team, introduces Canarytokens, an open-source project that creates trip wires: decoy documents, credentials and other artifacts that alert the defender when an attacker uses them. He explains that the team's research involved many dead ends, and that documenting failed approaches is as useful as the final result. The goal was a simple, low-noise alert when a rarely run Windows command, such as nltest or klist, executes on hosts that cannot run endpoint tooling.

The team first tried DOSKey macros, which were limited to individual user profiles, and then Windows process auditing with event 4688, which produced too much volume to be practical. They settled on Image File Execution Options, a registry debugger setting that attackers have used for persistence. When the watched program exits, a monitor process runs a PowerShell command that encodes the computer name and username into a DNS lookup. Along the way they hit a collision with a percent-C token in the monitor command and a mismatch between 32-bit and 64-bit registry views.

Smith covers the caveats: renaming a binary evades the trip wire, installing the key requires administrative rights, repeated DNS lookups need suppression, and watching cmd or PowerShell would create a loop. Usernames and hostnames appear in clear text in the alert. The talk ends by suggesting short-lived enumeration commands as good candidates and pointing to event log 3000 for correlation.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S14: Hey Yara, Let's Hunt For Some Vulnerabilities!

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S03: The Yandex Leak: How a Russian Search Giant Uses Consumer Data
talks.teaser: Walks through leaked Yandex source code to show how analytics SDKs and ad-profiling tools link user data to identities.
talks.summary:
In early 2023, about 45 GB of source code from the Russian search company Yandex was posted on a hacking forum. Yandex confirmed the code was theirs but denied it was a hack, blaming a former employee. The speaker, a privacy engineer, explains the company's business model across more than 90 services and the political pressure it has faced since Russia's invasion of Ukraine. That pressure includes a state-linked golden share, the sale of its news assets, and reported demands from security services for user data.

The middle of the talk walks through code for the AppMetrica analytics SDK and the Crypta behavioral analytics system. The speaker describes hashed device identifiers that still stay linkable, location fields that include altitude, speed and direction, and Wi-Fi network names used to group records into households. Crypta, by contrast, builds demographic ad segments from data across Yandex apps and ties identifiers to a single Yandex ID. Its code also includes matching logic that syncs fingerprinting events with several Russian telecom providers, one of them state-owned. The speaker notes that it is not always possible to tell from code alone whether a given component was actively used.

The main takeaway is that hashing and anonymization claims weaken once data is joined with other identifiers, a pattern the speaker describes as the mosaic effect. For practitioners, the lesson is to check which third-party SDKs sit inside their apps, what data they collect, and where that data is sent, since ownership and jurisdiction can change later.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S04: From RTFM to RCE: An Unexpected Dive into the Remote Desktop Protocol
talks.teaser: Shows how reading RDP Gateway protocol documentation uncovered a code execution flaw, a forgeable cookie and logging abuse.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the Remote Desktop Protocol and asks what can be found by working through its published specifications before reaching for debugging tools. The speaker cites an internet scan that turned up over 5 million RDP servers exposed online, and says the long-lived protocol is a prime target. The research focused on the RDP Gateway, which tunnels client connections through to internal servers.

The first case came from the specification's description of messages that carry Unicode strings. Two messages were documented without a null terminator, and sending them that way crashed the client. Further analysis showed a heap overflow caused by an off-by-one error, which the speaker tied to code execution on a client that connects through a malicious gateway. A second case involved the cookie used to create side channels. It is a PKCS7-signed blob, and the gateway checked the signature but not who signed it, so a self-signed certificate was accepted. That allowed forged user names, server names and ports, enabling Event Viewer log injection, UDP server-side request forgery, a UDP amplification effect and syslog flooding through broadcast. The flaw dated back to Windows Server 2008. A third finding involved the deprecated DTLS 1.0 version still being used, spotted in Wireshark.

The closing advice was to read the manual, treat proprietary protocols as partly documented and partly open, and report findings early rather than building a full exploit.
