talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S02: A Touch of Pwn: Attacking Windows Hello Fingerprint Authentication
talks.teaser: Explains full Windows Hello fingerprint bypasses on three laptops, from weak sensor protocols to USB man-in-the-middle attacks.
talks.summary:
Jesse Toano and Teimo describe a research engagement, handed to them by Microsoft's offensive research team, to see whether three Windows Hello fingerprint sensors could be defeated under a physical-access threat model. The targets were a Dell Inspiron with a Goodix sensor, a Lenovo ThinkPad with a Synaptics sensor, and a Surface Pro X with a fingerprint type cover. All three match fingerprints on the sensor chip, so the work focused on the chip, the host driver and the secure device connection protocol (SDCP) meant to authenticate the sensor, rather than on fake fingerprints. Privilege escalation was out of scope.

On the Goodix device, the Linux driver had dropped SDCP's security steps, so enrollment accepted arbitrary IDs. An unauthenticated configuration packet selected which template database the sensor used, and the team rewrote that packet in a debugger so Windows matched against the Linux database. Existing USB tooling mishandled zero-length packets, so they built their own man-in-the-middle rig on a Raspberry Pi. On the ThinkPad, SDCP was off by default, and the custom TLS-style channel had implementation flaws. The session key came from BIOS product name and serial number, which made the sensor reachable for enrollment. The Surface type cover used a simple protocol that could be bypassed by recording and replaying a SID, with a USB wake-up descriptor issue complicating the gadget implementation.

The researchers reported full authentication bypass on all three targets. Their takeaways were that vendor implementations varied widely, that SDCP's scope is narrow and leaves other commands and unauthenticated paths exposed, and that the sensor firmware looked fragile. They flagged memory corruption and hardware-level secret extraction as future work, and advised administrators to confirm that SDCP is actually enabled.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. Day 2 Keynote: Jason Haddix
talks.teaser: Walks through how threat actors breached a large gaming company using stolen cookies, and what defenders changed afterward.
talks.summary:
This keynote is a case study of a serious intrusion at Ubisoft, a video game company with about 22,000 staff, carried out by several threat actors. The speaker, who was the company's CISO at the time, explains that the entry point was stolen session cookies and credentials bought cheaply from underground marketplaces. Many of these came from personal or home laptops used during the shift to remote work. Once inside, the attackers spent weeks reading internal wikis, tickets, logs and developer tooling to learn the network, and avoided the noisy techniques that usually trigger EDR alerts. Their aim was partly disruption rather than ransom, and they deleted virtual machines and backups.

The middle of the talk covers the response. Remaining devices moved to managed hardware with EDR, and personal antivirus was reimbursed for staff. Web session cookies were shortened to 24 hours and mobile sessions to one week. MFA changes were limited to trusted networks, number matching and login location maps were added, and hardware keys were rolled out in phases. Admin panels were placed behind jump hosts, and VM deletion on ESXi was blocked unless verified by hand. A secrets management program used pre-commit hooks, a vault with credential rotation, and repository scanning. The team also monitored dark web markets with sock puppet accounts and paid bug bounties for leaked company credentials.

The closing takeaways are to treat downtime as a core threat model, to lean on identity and session controls, to run secrets management as a funded program, and to watch criminal markets for your own data. The speaker also stresses sharing threat intelligence with peers and with local FBI field offices during a breach.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S20: Unmasking Azure Based Adversaries
talks.teaser: Walks through investigating a leaked Azure service principal secret and detecting anomalous service principal activity at scale.
talks.summary:
Azure service principals act as non-human identities. They are local instances of app registrations that authenticate with client secrets or certificates, and they often carry far more access than their owners expect. The speakers, from Microsoft's hunt and data science teams, explain how these objects differ from older service accounts, how managed identities reduce credential exposure, and where a service principal's permissions are hidden across the portal, Graph and the Azure CLI.

For incident response, they walk through a scenario where a client secret has leaked. Sign-in logs showed invalid secret attempts followed by a successful Graph sign-in, then access to Key Vault and a custom app. Audit logs revealed admin consents and a role assignment that made the service principal a global admin. Checking API permissions and subscription role assignments showed which resources were reachable, while Cloud app events and Azure activity logs were used to baseline normal operations against the suspicious ones. Remediation differs by identity type: service principal credentials should be revoked and sign-ins disabled, and access should be scoped to individual resources rather than broad owner or contributor roles on a subscription.

On the detection side, the data science approach groups service principals by daily sign-in volume and applies Local Outlier Factor to find outliers within each peer group. Statistical thresholds on resources accessed and unusual errors, followed by a scoring step, narrow the results further. On one sample day the pipeline reduced about 92,000 active service principals to 4,000, then 140, then 22. Merging with Entra's first-party risk detections brought it to about two results per month. The takeaways are to put guardrails around non-person accounts, prefer Key Vault and managed identities, and use the available logs to hunt for unusual service principal behaviour.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S13: AI Security: Like Hacking in the 90s
talks.teaser: Shows unauthenticated file-read and code-execution bugs in popular AI tools like MLflow, H2O and Ray.
talks.summary:
The talk frames AI and machine learning security as a new domain that repeats the usual arc of technology shifts. The presenters argue that AI engineering teams are attractive targets, since their tools hold data, models and cloud credentials yet often go untested. Dan McInerney, a red team researcher, says many tool developers favour convenience, so the same few API flaws recur, including file inclusion, request forgery and remote code execution.

Case studies follow. In MLflow, a default install without authentication let him read server files such as SSH and cloud keys through a few API calls, and a patch was bypassed within weeks. H2O-3 exposed a file browser and allowed reading and overwriting files without login. In Ray, he and a colleague found several file and request forgery flaws plus anonymous code execution within 30 minutes, yet the maintainers rated the reports informational. He added that common scanners lack checks for these AI tools.

The closing advice is that pen testers should prioritise AI engineering hosts, since one MLflow server can expose credentials and data, and that firewalls offer little protection against email lures. Because trained models are hard to patch, a flaw in a widely used library can leave every stored model exposed until it is retrained. The speakers invited researchers to the bug bounty program, with more reports pending disclosure.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. Day 1 Keynote: John Lambert
talks.teaser: The address links defining incidents to log pivoting, exhaustive hunting, honeypot deception, and exploit-failure indicators.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens by framing a long security career as a sequence of defining incidents, from early worm eras through modern supply-chain and ransomware cases. Incidents are treated as ground truth: they reveal what defenders must study, and many breaches stay hidden until someone asks the right question.

The technical core argues that defense has a broad toolkit, not a single shield. Every contact leaves traces in logs across logical layers, and pivoting joins endpoint, identity, network, and application data like a graph. Hunting should zoom beyond the corporate perimeter into threat intelligence feeds, pursue leads until pivots are exhausted (illustrated with sticky keys persistence and follow-on attacker behaviors), and use long-retained logs for time-travel detection at kill-chain bottlenecks. Honeypots can induce failures to extract more adversary indicators, while crash telemetry and partial exploit artifacts—nop sleds, getPC stubs, API resolution—can signal professional tradecraft or unknown vulnerabilities.

The closing sections shift to teamwork under pressure: trust, empathy, and calibrated escalation matter as much as tooling. Career longevity comes from restorative hobbies, balance, and community relationships that enabled responses such as SolarWinds discovery and collaboration across vendors, plus researcher partnerships that amplified fixes through coordinated disclosure programs.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. Lighting Talks Day 1
talks.teaser: Lightning speakers share YouTube education tactics, developer security habits, threat-hunting training, and richer manual IOC formats.
talks.summary:
The first segment follows a bug-bounty-focused YouTube creator who explains why the gap between installing Burp and earning a first bounty motivated her channel. She outlines mind-map planning, one clear learning objective per video, slide-driven recording for consistency, template workflows, microphone and thumbnail basics, and steady uploads aimed especially at beginners worldwide who report first bugs and bounties from her material.

A GitHub security lab director frames the one-security-person-per-hundred-developers imbalance with a vegetables metaphor. He urges explaining value, setting requirements where possible, and making security work pleasant: high-precision CodeQL query sets for developers, alerts as pull-request comments instead of PDFs or ticket floods, and coding assistants that walk through SQL injection on the developer’s own snippet through parameterized fixes. A KC7 nonprofit director describes building threat-actor profiles into an engine that generates realistic data so students and career changers practice hunting, pivoting, and mapping behaviors without needing a prior industry job.

The closing segment targets manual indicator sharing beyond bare IP or domain lists. The speaker advocates compact enriched lines—hostname with resolution and TTL, registration and nameserver context, IPs with autonomous-system detail—and points to open utilities plus MISP objects for richer automated exchange.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S15: Breach Path Busters: Using Graphs and AI to Decode Cyber Threats
talks.teaser: Shows how Azure red team graph tooling maps attack paths across cloud permissions, and how defenders query them with AI.
talks.summary:
Engineers from the Azure red team and MSRC threat hunting explain how attackers find multi-step routes through cloud resources, and how their teams scale that work. The red team's internal graph, first built around 2015 and rebuilt several times since, holds 265 million nodes covering access groups, subscriptions, key vaults, and Azure DevOps projects and repositories. A worked example follows a certificate left in a pre-production key vault that leads to a production service principal with access to valuable data.

Manual path hunting cannot keep up with thousands of services, so the team turns observed attack techniques into pattern graphs, converts each resulting path into an optimized query, and runs those queries across the map. The speaker reported seven attack vectors yielding 24 patterns and 120 queries across five breach path types. Results are ranked by blast radius, internet exposure and severity, then turned into one-step remediation tickets so service owners can fix the most serious paths first.

On the defensive side, the threat hunting team wrapped the graph in a software library and notebooks for blast radius and breach path questions, then added a natural language interface built on large language models that generates the queries and renders results as graphs, tables or summaries. The closing advice is to treat infrastructure as a connected system, identify the relationships attackers traverse, and remove architectural weak points through measures such as ephemeral secrets, zero trust and least privilege.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S11: How to Make AI Comply
talks.teaser: Outlines how to build guardrails, threat models and prompt safety testing into generative AI systems before and after release.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's path into Microsoft research and a 2017 project that tried to make a social media bot act like a teenage girl. The speaker says the abusive replies that later spread from that bot came from people who found a debug API and sent messages through it, not from the model writing them on its own. That episode frames the argument that a large language model is only one component of a larger application, and that familiar security habits such as threat modeling, code review and input filtering still apply.

The middle section reviews the risks seen in chat assistants from 2023, including fabricated facts and hostile or manipulative replies, along with the policy context in the United States, such as executive orders on software supply chain attestation and the NIST AI risk management framework. The speaker recommends setting company principles and building a cross-functional group that includes security, privacy, legal, HR, and a dedicated responsible AI role. Practical advice includes defining explicit access boundaries, keeping a human approving any action a model takes, and testing across permutations and languages. The speaker also suggests describing allowed scope rather than listing excluded topics, since exclusion lists tend to miss variations.

The closing section argues that prompt safety testing looks more like social engineering than classic injection testing. Teams should monitor sessions, detect problems, retune and redeploy quickly, and run safety reviews before launch rather than after. The talk ends by stressing that people, not AI systems, must set, enforce and monitor these controls.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. Lighting Talks Day 2
talks.teaser: Four lightning segments explore agile security policy, K-12 curricula, women-in-security groups, and live NTLM v1 domain compromise.
talks.summary:
The session strings together four BlueHat lightning presentations on distinct security practice areas. The opening segment argues that static, compliance-heavy policy cycles lag behind modern threats, and maps Scrum roles, sprints, retrospectives, and a prioritized policy backlog onto cybersecurity doctrine so organizations can iterate while keeping risk analysis and regulatory baselines.

The next segments turn to people and pipelines. One presenter, a high school student, outlines a four-part plan to reshape K-12 education: a required fundamentals course spanning secure coding basics, cryptography, threat modeling, and familiar frameworks; an advanced elective tied to certifications; train-the-trainer support for teachers; and internship pathways that admit high schoolers rather than only college enrollees. Another speaker, a senior security program manager, describes standing up a women-in-security group with no initial budget—forming leadership, writing a mission statement, recruiting through chat channels and kickoff meetings, running internal speaker series and technical sessions such as threat modeling, and adjusting offerings from member feedback.

The closing segment is a live offensive demonstration. Using coercion to force a domain controller to authenticate with NTLM version one, the presenter captures the challenge-response, explains how NT responses embed crackable DES key material, walks through hashcat and helper utilities to recover the machine account hash, and uses pass-the-hash style access to perform DC Sync. The practical takeaway is that environments still allowing NTLM v1 at low LAN Manager compatibility settings remain vulnerable to full domain credential theft.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S23: Inside MSRC Cloud Vulnerability Management
talks.teaser: Follows a vulnerability report through MSRC's triage, cloud incident response, and coordinated disclosure steps.
talks.summary:
The speakers, both from Microsoft's Security Response Center, explain how a vulnerability report moves through MSRC. Reports arrive by email or through the researcher portal, and a team of about 30 people reviews every valid submission by hand. Accepted cases get a case manager and move to a verification and mitigation group that confirms the issue and sets severity, while the owning engineering team is notified to schedule a fix. Bounty decisions run alongside, and internal reporters are acknowledged but not paid.

Release timing came next. Fixes can take about five weeks to prepare for the regular patch day, while cloud fixes ship whenever they are ready, and CVEs are currently issued for cloud issues only when customers must take action. Researchers are asked to wait 30 days after a patch before public disclosure so customers can update, and MSRC reviews drafts of publications before they go out.

When a report uncovers an actual security incident, such as cross-tenant data access or an attempt to reach a service's back end, an internal escalation engages the incident response team. They deploy a carefully vetted hot fix, investigate everything the researcher touched, and notify affected customers and governments within contractual and regulatory deadlines. Takeaways for engineering teams include raising alarms early, providing service experts to investigators, keeping logs long enough, and resetting any secrets the researcher could have used.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S10: Exploring the Windows Registry as a Powerful LPE Attack Surface
talks.teaser: Walks through reverse engineering the Windows kernel registry and the bug classes that enable local privilege escalation.
talks.summary:
The talk treats the Windows registry as a local attack surface, where a bug in its kernel implementation can let a low-privileged user reach kernel-level rights. The speaker, a Project Zero researcher, explains that the registry code has grown from a simple design in Windows NT 3.1 into a large mix of decades-old and recent code. Features such as registry virtualization, transactions and differencing hives add layers of state that interact in complicated ways.

The research method was to reverse engineer one self-contained component at a time in IDA, using public kernel symbols, then reason about its logic and how it interacts with other features. Three bug classes were highlighted: resource exhaustion that pushes hive and system-wide size quotas to reach rarely tested error paths, poor handling of partial failure in multi-step operations, and hive-format states that the loader accepts but the kernel never produces. A case study followed predefined keys, which slipped past safe handle wrappers in several system calls and led to crashes and a use-after-free. Microsoft later deprecated them. The speaker also described hive-based memory corruption, where out-of-bounds cell indexes can yield an address leak and arbitrary read and write, and walked through an exploit for one early bug that ended with a token swap to SYSTEM.

The work produced 33 issues in Project Zero's tracker, which were assigned 39 CVEs, most of them elevation of privilege. The takeaways are that the registry is underexplored and rewards deep, persistent analysis, and that vendors can gain the most by reducing attack surface and removing whole bug classes. Publishing more detailed public symbols would also save researchers considerable reverse engineering effort.

talks.title: BlueHat Oct 23. S07: Signed, Sealed, Delivered: The Rise of Signed Malicious Drivers
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning BlueHat Oct 23. S07: Signed, Sealed, Delivered: The Rise of Signed Malicious Drivers.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this BlueHat talk, Andrew Brandt (Principal Researcher at Sophos X-Ops) and Andreas Kluch (Senior Threat Researcher at Sophos) detail their investigation into malicious Windows kernel drivers abused in ransomware and malware campaigns. The presentation examines how threat actors transitioned from abusing legitimate, vulnerable drivers to successfully submitting malicious drivers through Microsoft's official Hardware Developer program to obtain legitimate Microsoft digital signatures.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Kernel Abuse**: Attackers require kernel execution to disable modern endpoint detection and response (EDR) agents before ransomware deployment. Attack vectors include abusing known vulnerable legitimate drivers or obtaining valid code-signing certificates.
- **Vulnerable Driver Abuse**: Threat actors leverage Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) tactics. Examples highlighted include Robinhood ransomware utilizing the vulnerable GIGABYTE driver (`gdrv.sys`) to disable Driver Signature Enforcement and execute an unsigned driver, and BlackByte ransomware abusing `RTCore64.sys` to perform arbitrary reads and writes in kernel memory to overwrite notify routine arrays (`PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine`).
- **Maliciously Signed Drivers**: Rather than relying solely on vulnerable third-party drivers or leaked certificates (such as leaked NVIDIA keys or fraudulent Chinese company certificates), attackers compromised the Microsoft Hardware Developer program pipeline to produce kernel drivers signed directly with Microsoft's Windows Hardware Compatibility certificate.

### Technical Details
- **Submission Pipeline Abuse**: Submitting drivers via the Windows Hardware Developer dashboard requires an Extended Validation (EV) or Organization Validation (OV) certificate, signing a `.cab` archive containing driver files, and passing Microsoft compatibility and security checks. Attackers successfully met these conditions to produce fully signed, trusted malicious drivers.
- **The EDR Killer Toolkit**: An investigation stemming from a Cuba ransomware incident revealed an EDR-killing driver paired with a loader (`steel.exe` / `z-stop`). The driver registered a symbolic link (`\??\kapc_helper_link1`) matching earlier burnt cigar / POORTRY tooling. Driven via custom IOCTLs, the driver parsed targeted process lists (such as a list containing 29 Sophos-specific processes out of 186 targets) and repeatedly terminated matched processes every 250 milliseconds.
- **Packing and Obfuscation**: In an anomaly for kernel-mode code, the malicious signed drivers were heavily obfuscated with runtime commercial packers, predominantly VMProtect and Themida, concealing malicious logic from standard inspection.
- **Hunting and Threat Landscape**: Telemetry and VirusTotal hunting uncovered multiple distinct malware categories carrying valid Microsoft or suspicious certificates. Beyond the POORTRY/burnt cigar variants, researchers identified:
  - **accpt rootkit**: An EDR killer specifically targeting Chinese anti-malware drivers.
  - **AFK Undead & Fsys**: Modular rootkits capable of monitoring and modifying SSL traffic and injecting browser content.
  - **NetFilter**: A network-monitoring sniffer rootkit that redirected traffic to external domains using domain generation algorithms (DGAs) under `.xyz` TLDs, with artifacts dating back to April 2021.

### Takeaways
- **Industry Collaboration & Disclosure**: Sophos coordinated through the Microsoft Active Protections Program (MAPP) and MSRC. When initial detection signatures generated hundreds of presumed false-positive notifications from Microsoft's signed catalog, deeper analysis proved that these flagged files were indeed malicious signed drivers.
- **Revocation and Remediation**: Microsoft remediated the threats across multiple updates, including Patch Tuesday advisories in late 2022 and July 2023. The incident highlighted Microsoft's use and subsequent documentation of `drivers.stl` to revoke and invalidate compromised driver certificates at scale.

talks.title: The BlueHat Podcast Episode 004: Dan Tentler (aka Viss)
talks.teaser: A veteran consultant revisits pre-industry defensive techniques and explains why fundamentals still anchor modern security architecture.
talks.summary:
The episode follows a long-tenured consultant from teenage bulletin-board experimentation through founding a small full-service security firm, using that history to frame a Blue Hat 2023 session on defending networks with approaches that predated today's product ecosystem.

Much of the conversation revisits that presentation's core argument: appliances and cloud controls often wrap ordinary stack components, so operators who understand nginx, scripting, fail2ban, and SSH brute-force logic can harden environments without drowning in dashboards. Examples include abusing parser pipelines on mail gateways and the DOS current-directory execution quirk on file-sharing boards. The guest urges simple triage questions when vulnerabilities land—shell or not, reachable or not—instead of juggling many scoring schemes, and describes turning widespread fail2ban sensors into a homegrown threat feed.

Later segments stress putting internet-visible assets behind VPNs, reading perimeter neglect as a signal of deeper hygiene problems, and learning fundamentals before chasing rebranded machine-learning marketing. The interview closes with practical outreach channels, conference travel habits, and a confirmed Security Fest appearance in Gothenburg.

talks.title: The BlueHat Podcast Episode 002: James Forshaw on Writing Your Own Tools
talks.teaser: A Project Zero researcher explains logic bugs, reverse engineering habits, and why writing your own security tools pays off.
talks.summary:
In this BlueHat podcast episode, the hosts talk with James Forshaw, a Google Project Zero researcher who has examined Microsoft products for about 13 years. He explains how logic vulnerabilities, which abuse the intended flow of an application, differ from memory corruption bugs, which are often found through fuzzing. He describes his own approach: pick areas that behave unexpectedly, then either reverse engineer the code in a disassembler or exercise the interface from outside and compare it with published protocol documentation.

He gives an example from documentation for a feature that was implemented both locally and remotely. The docs said to pass a specific number, which turned out to index a table that changed between Windows versions. Passing that value to the local implementation caused a crash, and the same crash occurred remotely. He argues that custom tooling saves time, helps pinpoint attack surface, and lets a researcher learn a technology they do not yet understand. Existing open-source tools can be hard to extend, so a quick tool may be faster. For beginners he suggests Python with a library that implements Windows protocols, and notes that .NET can help where application control is in place.

The conversation also covers his network protocol tool, which grew out of contracting work and informed his book on attacking network protocols. He closes with his upcoming BlueHat Israel talk on Windows authentication research, including debugging authentication components and Credential Guard, and his current focus on the Windows sandbox used by Chrome. He points listeners to Mastodon and to the issue trackers of his GitHub tools for follow-up questions.

talks.title: The BlueHat Podcast Episode 003: Cameron Vincent on Both Sides of Bug Hunting
talks.teaser: A former full-time bug bounty hunter recounts his path into Microsoft, the burnout he faced, and advice for newcomers.
talks.summary:
This episode features Cameron Vincent recounting how he got into security. As a child he modified an Xbox 360, and in 2016 he earned his first bug bounty payment, $900 for a subdomain takeover. He then hunted bugs full time for several years, focusing on web applications, where insecure direct object references made up about 30% of his submissions. He later joined Microsoft's security response team, where he now reviews reports from outside researchers.

The discussion moves to his BlueHat 2023 session, which he co-presented with a Microsoft colleague. It paired his hunting method for object reference flaws with a tool built to find the same issues automatically, and the pair noted a fixed case that came back as a regression. Vincent also described the isolation and constant pressure of bug bounty work, and the burnout that led him to step back until a former manager offered him a role at Microsoft.

For newcomers he recommends studying public disclosure reports, spending weeks learning a product before testing it, and using the free version of Burp Suite. He also advises recording video walkthroughs with submitted reports, taking real breaks, and staying in touch with the security community in person or online.

talks.title: BlueHat Seattle 2019 || I'm in your cloud: A year of hacking Azure AD
talks.teaser: Shows a year of Azure AD research: undocumented APIs, service principal abuse, privilege escalation and backdoors.
talks.summary:
Dirk-jan Mollema presents a year of research into Azure Active Directory, a service whose platform design is not publicly documented the way on-premises systems are, which makes outside analysis harder. The talk starts with how the service is organised: tenants, applications, and service principals, the permissions linking them, and how the portal exposes these objects compared with internal interfaces.

The middle covers the findings. Information gathering was possible through undocumented APIs. Mollema shows how applications and service principals can be abused: a principal with delegated or application permissions can reach mail and files, and holders of the application administrator role can add credentials to higher-privileged service principals and act as them. Other cases include escalation through limited roles, a conditional access policy change that is hard to spot in the standard portal, and the link to on-premises synchronisation, where synchronised accounts carry risk into the cloud. Some issues were fixed, while others follow from the architecture itself.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to review who holds application administrator and similar roles, watch changes to applications, service principals and conditional access policies, and treat synchronised identities as part of the cloud attack surface. Basic Azure AD and Office 365 knowledge is assumed.

talks.title: BlueHat Seattle 2019 || Modern Binary Analysis with ILs
talks.teaser: Explains why intermediate languages suit binary analysis and compares several IL designs with live plugin demos.
talks.summary:
Binary analysis works on compiled output, where variable names, types, and function boundaries are gone and must be inferred. The speakers argue that many of these gaps are undecidable, such as separating code from data or resolving indirect jumps, so analysis tools must plan for failures. Intermediate languages offer a smaller, more regular layer that can support analysis across architectures.

The survey compares IRs used for reverse engineering, including LLVM IR, Ghidra's P-code, IDA's microcode, radare's ESIL, and Binary Ninja's BNIL family. LLVM IR was built for emitting code rather than recovering it, though re-emitting lifted code for another architecture is an advantage. Before choosing an IL, the speakers suggest checking architecture and language coverage, lifting completeness, stack handling, and data-flow APIs.

Two demos followed on Binary Ninja. A crypto-constant plugin recognized MD5 and Kasumi constants in a library built from public source, and still found them after the constants were XORed, since it read values from the medium-level IL. A second plugin resolved functions loaded at runtime through dlsym and GetProcAddress, creating pointers that added cross-references a plain import list would miss. Analysis written against a tree-based IL can stay portable across platforms and architectures.

talks.title: BlueHat Seattle 2019 || Don't forget to SUBSCRIBE.
talks.teaser: Traces the path from JTAG shell access on an embedded device to a heap exploit chain in its UPnP service.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a consumer ARM-based network device whose firmware was not publicly available. The speaker found the FCC filing and internal photos, noticed unpopulated header pins that looked like JTAG, and wired them to an adapter. Using OpenOCD, he dumped memory from the running kernel, located the boot parameters, and redirected init so a shell started at boot.

With a shell, he reviewed the boot scripts and focused on the UPnP daemon handling WPS. The main binary was not position independent, and while the heap and libraries were randomized and DEP was enabled, the main binary's fixed addresses limited the options. An oversized timeout header in a subscribe request led to a crash, and changing the subscription duration gave him control of a register holding attacker data. He then sprayed the heap with subscription allocations, used a base64-encoded SOAP field to place gadgets without bad characters, and pivoted the stack with a memcpy gadget because a load-multiple instruction rejects the stack pointer. The chain eventually returned a shell after about 25 minutes.

The talk ends with a failed attempt to pivot through a local TCP service, followed by a test-case harness that discovers UPnP services and fuzzes them automatically. It rediscovered a known out-of-bounds read in miniupnpd caused by misusing snprintf's return value, which was already fixed upstream. The takeaway is to automate repetitive manual checks and save the exact request that caused each crash.

talks.title: BlueHat Seattle 2019 || Kubernetes Practical Attack and Defense
talks.teaser: Walks through a live, demo-driven attack on an intentionally vulnerable Kubernetes cluster, from pod compromise to cloud takeover.
talks.summary:
The speaker, Jay Beale, opens with a short overview of Kubernetes from an attacker's point of view. He covers the control plane, including the API server, the etcd state store, controllers and the scheduler, and the worker nodes running the kubelet and a container runtime. Each of these is a place where a misconfiguration can be abused. The rest of the session is a live demo against a deliberately vulnerable cluster, with each stage framed as defeating a character from a movie.

The attack starts with a web app that passes user input into a shell command, which gives remote command execution and a shell inside a pod. From there the default service account token is used to check what the pod is allowed to do. A neighbouring microservice that was not reachable from outside is then used to run commands, and a label-based service selector is abused by launching a rogue pod with matching labels, so that traffic meant for a backend service is redirected to the attacker. That yields another service account token. A Node.js serialization flaw in one microservice gives code execution, and an unauthenticated Redis instance that had been exposed inside the cluster leads to a node. From the node, the cloud metadata API returns instance credentials, a cluster state bucket in object storage holds admin tokens, and a pod that mounts the host filesystem gives root on the node. A tool called Peratis automates many of these checks.

The speaker stresses that none of these steps needed a CVE; they came from configuration. He closes with defenses that would have blocked parts of the chain: network policies to limit pod traffic and cloud API egress, pod security policies that stop host mounts and privileged containers, Linux capability limits, seccomp and AppArmor profiles, read-only root filesystems, and a service mesh that enforces identity and encryption between pods.

talks.title: BlueHat Seattle 2019 || Are We There Yet: Why Does Application Security Take So Long?
talks.teaser: Uses scan data from 85,000 applications to show how flaw fixing times vary with scan frequency and security debt.
talks.summary:
The talk asks why fixing application security flaws takes so long, drawing on a yearly research report built from scan results for about 2,300 customers and more than 85,000 applications, collected from April 2018 to March 2019. The speaker explains that the scanning service sees the code it checks, which gives the data its scale, and lists the biases that come with it, including customer selection, the languages and frameworks the tool supports, and missing context such as business criticality.

Rather than relying on simple averages, the analysis uses survival curves to show the chance that a flaw is still open after a given time. Overall, 56% of flaws were eventually fixed, and 75% of severity five flaws were. High-profile categories such as SQL injection were among the slowest to fix, and severity, exploitability and business criticality showed little link to fix time. Developers appeared to work on whatever was most recent in front of them, with about a 21% chance of a flaw being fixed in its first month. The speaker also introduces security debt, the gap between flaws found and flaws fixed, which grew on average and grew fastest where scanning was bursty.

On DevOps, the speaker uses scan frequency as a rough proxy for automation. Applications scanned daily had a median fix time three times faster than those scanned annually or monthly, although debt still built up. Only about 5% of applications were scanned weekly or more often. Steady scanning reduced debt over time, while irregular and bursty scanning, such as periodic security sprints, did not. The takeaway is that security automation needs to keep pace with DevOps adoption.

talks.title: BlueHat Seattle 2019 || Building Secure Machine Learning Pipelines: Security Patterns and Challenges
talks.teaser: Shows how LinkedIn applies access, encryption and container controls across each stage of its machine learning pipelines.
talks.summary:
LinkedIn's security team explains how it secures machine learning pipelines behind features such as member network building, job recommendations, feed content and abuse detection. The talk splits the ML lifecycle into experimentation, training and evaluation, deployment, and serving, and maps the risks in each stage. Examples include unauthorized data access and leakage during feature engineering, untracked intermediate datasets during training, unintended model publication, personalized models exposing member data, and misconfigured inference services vulnerable to resource exhaustion.

For each stage the presenters describe controls: role- and rule-based access control, encryption at rest and in transit, a metadata hub that annotates feature sensitivity, PII-detecting classifiers, dual verification with multi-factor authentication for model deployment, synthetic data in test environments, and benchmark checks with model health monitoring. They also cover the gap between offline Hadoop and Kerberos jobs and online services using mutual TLS, bridged by a translator service that issues tokens, and a planned move of compute and storage to Azure. For deep learning, containerized GPU pipelines bring risks such as vulnerable images, anonymous Kubernetes API access, open inter-container traffic and privileged containers, addressed through image certification, registry authentication, cluster segregation, audit logging and least privilege.

The takeaways are to segregate pipelines into security tiers based on workload sensitivity, keep a metadata system that links each model to its features and their sensitivity, and monitor continuously for vulnerabilities and performance degradation. Identity and access management and key management form the core security infrastructure, and automating controls lets them scale.

talks.title: BlueHat Seattle 2019 || The cake is a lie! Secret world of malware | cheats in video games
talks.teaser: Explains how game cheats reuse malware techniques, from obfuscation to kernel access, and the privacy trade-offs of anti-cheat tools.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with historical examples of cheating, from a famous football goal to a 1980s arcade record that a reverse engineer disputed, before turning to video games as a business. The speaker cites a League of Legends tournament with more than 100 million viewers, industry revenue figures for 2017 and 2018, and a projection of 160 for the current year. A 2013 World of Warcraft bot sold for 25 dollars to about 100,000 buyers, and the speaker describes how a lawsuit from Blizzard ended with the seller losing six million.

The middle section covers how cheats are sold, often as subscriptions or cheating-as-a-service with promised undetectability. Because many games trust the client to keep latency low, cheats can exploit that trust. The speaker shows that cheats use the same tools malware authors rely on: commercial protectors, code obfuscation, exploits for kernel access, rootkit-like hiding from anti-cheat, and process injection. Anti-cheat vendors need deep visibility into a player's processes and memory, which raises privacy concerns similar to those antivirus products have faced. Publishers often use delayed bans so cheat developers cannot learn what was detected.

The speaker argues that cheating is a growing multi-million-dollar illegal economy and that security researchers are well placed to study it, bridging a gap between the gaming and security communities. A research paper on the topic was announced as forthcoming. The main takeaway for practitioners is that game cheats are a real malware-style problem worth analysing, and that anti-cheat design has to balance detection against user privacy.

talks.title: BlueHat Seattle 2019 || The good, the bad & the ugly of ML based approaches for ransomware detection
talks.teaser: Shows how adversarial GAN-generated file activity can evade ML ransomware detectors, and which platform defenses could help.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at using machine learning to detect crypto ransomware, focusing on the encryption stage of its life cycle. The speakers describe collecting file I/O telemetry from bare-metal lab systems that ran ransomware samples, including event types, targeted file regions, and entropy changes. These events were mapped into integer sequences, zero-padded to a common length, and used to train seven classifiers. A TextCNN model performed best, and training another classifier on the TextCNN feature space improved accuracy, false positive rate, and related scores.

The second half turns to adversarial machine learning. The team trained a generative adversarial network to produce malicious-looking event sequences that could fool the detectors, and used two quality checks, one per sample and one per batch, to confirm the samples still behaved maliciously. Of roughly 5,000 generated samples, most classifiers missed the majority, while one support vector machine variant resisted. Analysis of decision boundaries showed the adversarial samples landing on the benign side in the TextCNN feature space. Concept drift and time variance were raised as further concerns for deployed models.

The speakers then suggested platform defenses, such as richer telemetry like processor trace, trusted execution to protect model weights from tampering, and persistent memory for finer access control. Their takeaway is that robustness matters as much as accuracy when ML guards security-critical systems, and that detection should be paired with local backups so critical systems can recover quickly.

talks.title: GRAPH FOR SECURITY WORKSHOP || Statistics Graphs Finding Bad Guys, Joshua Neil
talks.teaser: Shows how statistical scoring and graph analysis combine weak endpoint and network signals to expose attackers.
talks.summary:
The talk shows how a data science team behind Microsoft Defender's endpoint detection uses statistics and graphs to find attackers in enterprise networks. Nodes are computers, users or other entities, and edges are observed communications such as network flow records. Attackers rarely reveal their behaviour and have many possible paths, so the team models what is normal and scores deviations instead of relying on labelled data.

Examples cover several stages. Failed RDP logins to a machine are modelled with a zero-inflated negative binomial model that includes seasonality, and a one-minute burst of logins stands out as a successful brute-force attempt. New communication edges are scored by combining how often a source starts new connections with how often a destination receives them. PowerShell scripts are converted into numeric embeddings, and their distance from a supervised classifier's decision line becomes a node score. Each signal alone is too weak to alert on, but linked on a graph they reveal an attack path.

To locate the malicious subgraph, the talk covers a greedy walk from the lowest-scoring element, template enumeration of paths and stars with its multiple-testing problem, and spectral methods over adjacency matrices and graph time series. Attack durations range from minutes to years, so cumulative control-chart statistics help catch both fast and slow activity. The takeaway is to score deviations on every node and edge and then connect those scores, while handling the false positives that path enumeration produces.

talks.title: GRAPH FOR SECURITY WORKSHOP || Graphical Analysis for Security, Gabe Bassett
talks.teaser: Contrasts graph and table models for security intelligence, covering query fit, visualization pitfalls, and breach-report path analytics.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames graph use in security as a pragmatic choice driven by how data is shaped and how questions are asked, not because relationships always demand a graph database. He traces experience from early intelligence work through Excel-based prototypes to large-scale breach analytics, emphasizing trade-offs: linked structures versus matrices, vertex-style traversals versus SQL-like filters, and the cost of hanging heavy properties on nodes.

The middle of the talk separates useful graph thinking from seductive but unreadable pictures. Small, labeled graphs, topology-style structural views, and narrative visuals (for example proxy auto-config centrality or staged malware spread) can steer executives; oversized hairballs cannot. He advocates filtering, grouping, layout experiments, and sometimes exporting tabular results instead of forcing a picture. Years of DBIR-style work moved from decorative attack graphs toward path overlays and mitigation questions—such as which single control blocks the most routes and why most adversaries abandon after one failed tactic while a minority chain alternatives.

Practitioners should match storage and query patterns to the job, treat visualization as communication—not proof—and prefer simple graph algorithms when the question is clear. Building graphs in memory from flat data, then discarding them, often scales better than assuming a permanent graph store is required.

talks.title: GRAPH FOR SECURITY WORKSHOP || Scaling Graphical Analysis, Leo Meyerovich
talks.teaser: Shows how graph models turn SOC logs and APIs into interactive investigations, with GPU scaling and a trafficking case study.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the cost of manual investigation. Analysts pivot by hand between SIEM logs, threat intelligence lookups and endpoint data, then repeat the same work when the time window grows. The speaker argues that a hypergraph built from log events, combined with a virtual graph over vendor APIs, gives responders one model they can click through. A notebook demo showed query results from Splunk and Kusto becoming an interactive graph, with edges colored by time to show what happened first.

The middle section covers automation and where graphs fit. Pivot steps can be saved as workflows that run from an alert, and the generated queries are often more thorough than what an analyst would type manually. Graphs work well for scoping, following progression over time and showing relationships, but the speaker stressed that they are not the answer to every problem. For a case study with an anti-trafficking group, business records and online reviews were scored with machine learning, then a simpler clustering method was run on the same data. Expanding the linked company metadata revealed a wider network of phone numbers and individuals. The speaker also described GPU-backed dataframes and graph algorithms that handle billions of edges interactively.

The closing part gives practical advice for graph projects. Many data projects fail, so the speaker recommended starting with one user and one useful result, not a large platform build. Teams should avoid asking people to remove existing tools, and should work first with a small group of enthusiastic champions. Shared playbooks for common incident types can encode best practice and set coverage goals for a team.

talks.title: GRAPH FOR SECURITY WORKSHOP || Finding your blast radius your peers, Sridhar Periyasamy
talks.teaser: Explains how peer groups and blast-radius graphs in Azure add context to alerts, helping analysts cut false positives.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the cost of false positives, which the speaker estimates at about 21,000 hours a year and roughly 1.3 million dollars for a midsize company. The proposed remedy is enriching alerts with metadata that adds context, aiming to cut false positives, shorten resolution time and push defenders to reason in graphs.

The first enrichment is peers, the users a person most often works with, derived from shared group membership rather than directory hierarchy, since only about 40 percent of companies in Azure have hierarchy data set up. Nested groups are counted, very large groups are ignored, and smaller shared groups carry more weight. Given an alert, activity matching what peers normally do can be suppressed as likely benign, while a mismatch warrants investigation.

The second enrichment is blast radius, the privileges an entity holds including hidden and transitive ones, which shows the full impact if that entity is compromised. It is modelled as a directed graph linking users, groups, subscriptions and service principals. In the example, revoking a user's subscription access means cutting each edge, including two groups with read access and a service principal. Service principal activity appears in audit logs under the principal rather than the person behind it, so these identities are a useful focus. The speaker noted the feature is in private preview for Microsoft Sentinel, built on Log Analytics.

talks.title: GRAPH FOR SECURITY WORKSHOP || Graphs in Security, Ian Hellen
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding GRAPH FOR SECURITY WORKSHOP || Graphs in Security, Ian Hellen.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at the Graph for Security Workshop, Ian Hellen, a principal security engineer at Microsoft, discusses how Python Jupyter notebooks and entity-centric graphing techniques can be applied to cybersecurity investigations and threat hunting. While referencing the classic John Lambert quote that "attackers think in graphs, defenders think in lists," Hellen emphasizes that defenders are increasingly shifting toward graph-based thinking. Rather than relying on static tables or spreadsheets, analysts can use notebooks to orchestrate investigation workflows, extract suspicious subgraphs from massive telemetry sets, and avoid analyst fatigue.

### Key Topics
- **Extracting Attacker Graphs from Telemetry:** Modern security operations are inundated with granular logs from agents and cloud services. Hellen identifies three ways to isolate suspicious subgraphs: appending detections/inferences to label nodes and edges, identifying known-bad indicators (such as C2 IP addresses from threat intelligence), and detecting anomalous graph structures or chained behaviors directly.
- **Graph Structure Anomaly Detection:** Hellen shares prior work analyzing corporate host-to-host lateral movement chains to identify attacks. He also highlights an approach by a former Google security team member using natural language processing (NLP) to model network syntax and identify anomalous graph paths as grammatical or vocabulary errors.
- **Advantages of Jupyter Notebooks:** Notebooks address the limitations of traditional investigation tools like Excel or ephemeral cloud query consoles (e.g., Azure Sentinel Log Analytics). Notebooks make query workflows repeatable, persist queries and retrieved data in a single document, support interactive visualizations, and serve as presentation media for technical and non-technical stakeholders.
- **MSTICPy Open-Source Toolkit:** Hellen showcases `msticpy`, a Python package designed to encapsulate complex security analysis tasks. Features include process command-line clustering, rarity index scoring to highlight uncommon logon sessions, layered network flow visualization, time-series anomaly detection, nested de-obfuscation (base64/gzip decoding), regex IoC extraction, and multi-provider threat intelligence enrichment (e.g., VirusTotal, X-Force, AlienVault OTX).

### Technical Details
Hellen demonstrates two "Entity Explorer" notebooks powered by Azure Sentinel and MSTICPy:
1. **Host Explorer:** Queries a Windows host to display interactive logon timelines and network flows categorized by Layer 7 protocols (such as inbound SSH and Terminal Services). Hellen demonstrates clustering 26,000 process execution events to compute a rarity index—the inverse of cluster size—allowing analysts to strip away repetitive administrative activity and surface rare events like user creation or group manipulation.
2. **Account Explorer:** Starts with a user account ("Ian") to dynamically map host logons, associated source IP addresses, automated alert correlation, geolocation/ASN data, and host-level alerts. Even without complex graph layouts, progressively appending alerts and threat intelligence transforms ordinary telemetry into an intuitive, explainable attacker subgraph.

### Takeaways
Jupyter notebooks combined with targeted, small-scale graphing provide a practical way to tame data overload in security operations. By automating repetitive queries, clustering noisy data, and layering threat intelligence directly into entity-centric graphs, analysts can build reproducible, explainable investigation artifacts that bridge the gap between low-level telemetry and actionable incident response.

talks.title: GRAPH FOR SECURITY WORKSHOP || Grapl - a Graph platform for detection response, Colin O'Brien
talks.teaser: Shows how a graph-based detection and response platform turns logs into linked entities for faster investigations.
talks.summary:
Grapl is an open-source detection and response platform that stores security data as a graph instead of isolated log lines. The speaker argues that attackers exploit relationships between processes, files, networks and users, which log searches and SIEM joins handle poorly. Logs become subgraphs with server-side identity resolution, so reused process IDs stop causing confusion, and these merge into one master graph in near real time.

Detections are Python analyzers that query this graph for suspicious structure. In one example, the signal is not the two normal binaries themselves but the unexpected parent-child link between them. Subgraphs carry risk scores, and lenses such as an asset view combine overlapping risks without extra correlation work. Because the rules are plain Python, they can be unit tested and linted, which helps alerts keep working as they are tuned.

For investigations, the speaker contrasts a hash-based lead that runs into search window limits and process ID recycling in a log store. In Grapl, an analyst opens a lens, creates an engagement and pivots through process ancestry with constant-time queries, while a Jupyter notebook records the steps for reuse and training. The platform runs largely on serverless AWS services and deploys with a short setup script. The takeaway is that modelling relationships directly makes detection and investigation faster and more compact.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Crafting synthetic attack examples from past cyber-attacks
talks.teaser: Explains how synthetic malicious and benign examples can balance training data for a detection model built from past attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why a machine learning model for detecting attacks in a large data center can be trained on too few real attack examples. The speakers, from the Office 365 security team, describe using supervised learning on labeled machines, with detections from several days flattened into per-machine feature vectors. Their confirmed malicious examples were scarce and clustered in a few machine roles, so a model trained on them looked strong on paper but would likely miss attacks on other roles.

To widen coverage they craft synthetic malicious examples with a method they call Cartesian bootstrapping. The signal from a malicious machine is overlaid on sampled benign machines, so one malicious example paired with several benign ones yields several new examples. In their Exchange workload case, close to 500 malicious examples grew to 84K after this step, covering more subpopulations. For validating a model on a small service, the speakers balance classes by oversampling benign examples, transplant malicious signals from other services onto them, and drop outliers such as a misconfigured machine producing tens of thousands of detections. They measure results with F-score, which combines precision and recall.

The takeaways are that penetration tests are a useful source of labeled attacks, and that when real malicious examples are few and do not cover the population, synthetic examples can help train and validate a more balanced model. The team retrains regularly and only promotes a new model if it holds up against the current one on incoming data.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Protecting the protector
talks.teaser: Explains how stacked ensembles harden malware classifiers against adversarial evasion, poisoned telemetry, and offline client probing.
talks.summary:
The speakers open with the scale of first-seen malware and why predictive machine learning must decide before attacks finish. They outline supervised and unsupervised learning in endpoint protection, contrasting fast client models with cloud metadata and sample-based deep learning, and why cloud contact limits offline adversarial probing.

They describe theoretical attack surfaces—poisoned training sets, feature evasion, model cloning, and black-box guessing—and two real incidents: malicious strings injected into clean files to trigger automation false positives via VirusTotal, and certificate-reputation stuffing against cloud telemetry. The core of the talk is model stacking: diverse base learners across features, algorithms, data slices, and cadence; Pearson correlation to avoid redundant inputs; linear stacking with probabilities rather than boolean votes; LightGBM as the meta-learner; and fixes for data leaks, sparse missing base outputs, volatile label distributions, training gates, and unsupervised cluster-distance features. They stress-test ensembles with JSMA feature perturbations and rogue random classifiers.

Production stacking reportedly yields roughly 10–15% more monthly detections on billions of daily queries. Case studies cover a small Canadian landscaping-invoice PDF phishing lure blocked when the ensemble overruled a weak PDF specialist, and polymorphic Bancos JavaScript in Brazil blocked when combined cloud signals crossed the ensemble threshold. Practitioners should spread capability across cloud and client, engineer classifier diversity before stacking, red-team the pipeline, and monitor training and block ratios continuously.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Badly behaving scripts
talks.teaser: Describes how malicious scripts fuel social-engineering attacks and how AMSI behavior logs feed client-cloud machine learning defenses.
talks.summary:
The session opens with how attackers rely on JavaScript, VBScript, and HTA files in phishing lures, exploit-kit downloaders, and fileless persistence, often obfuscated so each recipient gets a unique sample. Signature workflows lag large burst campaigns, so scalable alternatives matter when most malicious files reach only one customer.

The middle covers Anti-Malware Scan Interface integrations in Windows 10 script engines: content scans before compilation or execution, and behavior logs of COM calls that pause on execute-style statements until the installed product responds. Windows Defender sends featurized behavior—not full script text—to cloud models, using sandbox-derived COM and n-gram features reduced via MapReduce and learner-based selection to a few hundred signals, then trains on live telemetry because sandboxes and enterprise custom scripts skew labels.

Mustafa details clean-label heuristics, a lightweight client logistic model, and a cloud LightGBM ensemble where purpose-built AMSI features dominate; monotonic regression limits evasion by adding benign-looking noise. Practitioners should see AMSI as a vendor-neutral hook for script visibility, and pairing fast on-box triage with daily-updated cloud models as the workable pattern for first-seen script malware.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Massive scale usb device driver fuzz without device
talks.teaser: A scalable fuzzing pipeline targets thousands of Windows USB drivers without physical hardware by emulating devices in virtual machines.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with USB transfer types, enumeration on Windows, and how Plug and Play uses vendor and product IDs to pull third-party signed drivers from Windows Update. Prior USB security work largely depended on real gadgets, HID abuse, QEMU on open kernels, or slow in-the-middle bit flips, which poorly matches closed-source Windows at large scale.

The core idea is to harvest the driver corpus without plugging in hardware. The researcher spidered Microsoft’s vendor submission data, reverse engineered the update protocol from public specs, and collected on the order of four thousand installable driver packages, with catalog filtering and an IDA helper to prioritize kernel-relevant caps. Fuzzing runs through QEMU’s USB redirection and synthetic devices in a pool of Windows VMs, covering attach-time code, bulk replies, and IOCTL interfaces discovered by differencing device nodes, with crash dumps shared out for deduplication and kernel replay.

Reported outcomes exceed one hundred CVE IDs. The closing demo runs several virtual machines in parallel waiting for emulated plug events, then exercises drivers and logs progress. The practical lesson is that Windows’ automatic third-party USB driver supply chain is a high-yield, deviceless fuzzing surface when emulation replaces shelves of physical peripherals.

talks.summary: Luke Jennings surveys how attackers host implants entirely in memory without traditional exploits, beginning with reflective DLL injection and process hollowing, then tracing Sysmon signatures attackers bypass via atom bombing and anti-NtClose thread hijacks. He contrasts kernel-hooking limits with ETW and Defender ATP telemetry on Windows 10, and shows how memory forensics still catches meterpreter-style RWX regions even when API sequences vary. Jennings details real intrusions using DoublePulsar, WannaCry staging, Metasploit in energy-sector theft, and Isotope RAT kernel staging before discussing dotnet ghost pack loaders, JIT ETW visibility, and Gargoyle-like timer tricks that hide assemblies between executions.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Shoot first, ask later: strategies to defend the most phished country in the world
talks.teaser: Shows how blocking newly registered look-alike bank domains before attackers use them cut phishing exposure in Brazil.
talks.summary:
Fabio Cellini presents a proactive approach to phishing defense built on a timing gap: attackers often register look-alike domains well before they launch an attack. He reports that Brazil tops his vendor's phishing statistics, with 36 million attacks blocked there in 2017 and 40 million in the first seven months of 2018, and that most of these targeted financial institutions.

The method watches daily feeds of newly registered domains for brand keywords, mainly banks and card companies, and scores matches with WHOIS signals such as disposable email registrants, invalid registration data and domain age. String-similarity checks catch typosquats, and certificate transparency logs add Let's Encrypt certificates. Matches are blocked automatically. The false positive rate started near 7 percent and later dropped below 1 percent. One case involved a phone crew impersonating a bank; its domain was blocked a day before the call. After GDPR reduced WHOIS data, the team turned to passive DNS and registrant organization fields. Attackers answered with Unicode domains, and ambiguous keywords sometimes need human review.

He closes by urging other vendors to apply the same pre-emptive blocking, noting that keyword lists must be tuned per language and season, and that the approach currently covers four languages.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || The law of unintended consequences
talks.teaser: Shows how GDPR data minimization and erasure rules can strip the logs incident responders need, and how to plan around them.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how the EU General Data Protection Regulation affects security incident response. The speaker, from Microsoft's Security Response Center, says teams are deleting logs quickly because of GDPR, leaving responders without evidence to detect, attribute and act on attacks. Three scenarios illustrate this: a cross-site scripting breach where masked IP addresses stop attribution, repeat copyright infringers that DMCA rules require the provider to identify, and stolen intellectual property where logs purged after 29 days left a law enforcement request unanswerable.

The middle section covers GDPR basics, including data minimization, controller and processor roles, and rights such as access, erasure and objection. Several myths are challenged: deleting data early does not make an organisation compliant, since only transient data held 48 hours or less is helped, and personal data must relate to an identifiable natural person. Article 6 legitimate interest can justify keeping security logs, telemetry and memory dumps, but open-ended retention is not acceptable, so Microsoft documents this in a variance with a three-year retention period that can deny erasure requests for security data.

The closing advice is to ask engineers, system owners and lawyers which logs are truly needed, run tabletop exercises to find evidence gaps, and document legitimate interests before an incident. Responders should also push for retention and build audited storage so security data serves only investigations. The speaker stresses that GDPR is no excuse for weak security.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Improving Security Posture through Increased Agility
talks.teaser: Shows how Microsoft's Office 365 team built the Vanquish detection and remediation system to catch attackers in minutes.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Vanquish, a detection and remediation system Microsoft built to protect its Office 365 data center assets. The presenters argue that attackers can compromise systems within minutes, so detection and response need to move at a similar pace. Their design choices include deploying detection logic separately from telemetry collection so rules can ship several times a day, and treating detections as code with unit and acceptance tests so upstream changes cannot silently break alerts.

They describe a red team exercise in which Vanquish raised an alert about four minutes after the intrusion. Later forensic work produced a new detection within hours. A slower remediation effort let the attacker pivot between hosts, which led the team to build a subsystem that pushes remediation actions across the fleet for a given set of techniques. The measurement section covers service health such as data latency and Spark job status, endpoint coverage through heartbeats, and an internal tool called attack bot that runs real attacks on random hosts to confirm detections fire.

The machine learning part explains how anomaly detection filters normal behaviour and focuses on the long tail, while supervised models learn from past pen test examples. An automated pipeline retrains models and promotes them only when they beat the production version. In one October exercise, the model alerted on 10 of 24 compromised machines, some about 15 minutes before the attacker reached them. The main takeaways are to keep detection fast without impacting customers, to validate detections every day, and to automate tuning because the environment changes faster than hand-written rules can follow.
