talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Cybersecurity for the defense of democracy
talks.teaser: Outlines Microsoft's defending democracy program: campaign account protection, election integrity and disinformation research.
talks.summary:
The session, given by members of Microsoft's defending democracy program, opens with why cyber-enabled threats to elections now matter. The speakers note that nation-state attacks have grown in frequency and now target core democratic processes rather than only financial or military espionage targets. The program rests on four pillars: campaign security, election infrastructure, disinformation, and political advertising transparency.

The campaign section explains why political campaigns are attractive targets: they are often underfunded, build temporary IT quickly, and seldom have dedicated security staff. It introduces Account Guard, which leads with security education such as multi-factor authentication guidance. Opted-in individuals can also link personal accounts, so the organization is alerted if a known nation-state actor targets them. Participants also get early access to private previews. The speakers said that offering the service free to campaigns raised legal questions, and the election regulator reviewed the matter and approved it unanimously after a request.

The election integrity section compares the 2000 US recount controversy with the 2016 security incidents and describes elections as a system of systems spread across about 10,000 jurisdictions. Recommendations discussed include more funding, information sharing between federal and state officials, and post-election audits such as risk-limiting audits. The team also proposes threat modeling for elections to decide which vulnerabilities matter most. The session closed with calls to action: volunteer security skills, and weigh democratic impact in product security reviews.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Evolving chromes secuirty indicators
talks.teaser: Walks through how Chrome changed its HTTP warnings and lock icon, and why its URL display tests found no winner.
talks.summary:
Emily Schecter, a product manager on Google's Chrome security team, focuses on usable security. She explains that Chrome treats security UI as a research problem and walks through three user-facing changes. The first concerns negative indicators. Starting in January 2017, Chrome showed warnings on HTTP pages with password or credit card fields, which cut the fraction of such page navigations over HTTP by 23% on desktop. Chrome 62 extended the warning to any HTTP page where users enter data and to incognito mode, and Chrome 68 in July marked all HTTP pages as not secure.

The rollout was staged to limit warning fatigue, with a red treatment planned for HTTP data-entry pages in Chrome 70. A public transparency report tracked the top 100 sites defaulting to HTTPS, rising from 24 in January 2016 to 81. Success depended on advance outreach, an enterprise policy that let admins turn off the warnings, and support from Firefox, Safari and Let's Encrypt. On the positive side, Chrome removed the "secure" label and the HTTPS scheme from the default state, a change rolled back after issues. The lock was tinted gray, and an extended validation study was under way with no results yet.

Last, the URL research tested five layouts of the address bar against the Google sign-in page. None produced significant differences, and over half of respondents missed a spoofed URL, trusting it because it looked like Google. The takeaway is that security UI changes work best when browsers move together and are measured through staged rollouts.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Modern day entomology - examining the inner workings of the bug bazaar
talks.teaser: ZDI leaders share submission metrics, hacking-team procurement leaks, and cases where bought flaws disrupted government exploit stockpiles.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative as both a bug bounty conduit and an intelligence operation that buys proof-of-concept findings, coordinates vendor disclosure, and feeds signatures so customers may be protected well before public advisories land. The speaker walks through white, gray, and black markets for vulnerabilities—from vendor programs and brokers to government buyers and exploit-kit operators—and explains why rising tide effects from competing bounties increase legal researcher participation.

The middle of the talk is driven by internal ZDI metrics: quarterly submission growth, vendor and geography breakdowns (including SCADA HMI, virtualization, and high-profile vendors), and time-series charts showing how mitigations such as click-to-play, isolated heap protections, Flash end-of-life, and shifting browser versus Office versus PDF attack paths reshape researcher incentives. Leaked Hacking Team materials illustrate gray-market pricing, payment schedules, and inventory overlap with ZDI purchases, including a researcher who moved from the white market to brokered sales.

The close ties program telemetry to real-world impact: Shadow Brokers and CIA toolset examples where earlier ZDI-bought patches removed usable chains, BlackEnergy-related HMI fixes, and vbscript spikes preceding in-the-wild exploitation. The speaker argues mitigations and vendor patch velocity directly cool hot markets, notes ongoing zero-day exposure timelines across software verticals, and contends durable defense still depends on secure development—not bounties alone.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || The hitchhiker's guide to north korean malware
talks.teaser: Traces code reuse across North Korean malware families to link campaigns and build YARA rules from shared opcode patterns.
talks.summary:
The talk compares code similarity across a large collection of North Korean malware samples, dating from 2007 onward. The speakers used campaigns that several vendors had already confirmed as North Korean as a baseline, then widened the set. They first sketch the background they say shapes these operations: limited national resources, a state push from cyber espionage toward financially motivated attacks after sanctions, and overseas assignments for skilled operators who must send money home.

The middle of the talk focuses on attribution. The speakers describe false flags they encountered, including a leaked South Korean exercise tool that shared code with North Korean malware, and Swiss banking samples whose Russian strings came from machine translation even though all three were built in the same development environment. Their graph of shared code shows two clusters, one tied to Lazarus and another to a group referred to as group one two three. They also found code from a 2009 MyDoom wiper reappearing in the 2017 WannaCry attack. Compiler output and common libraries had to be filtered out, since shared third-party code can create misleading links.

For practitioners, the speakers recommend mapping observed behaviour to MITRE ATT&CK techniques and writing YARA rules from opcode sequences, with wildcards for registers and addresses that change between builds. They said this approach held up better than string-based rules and had produced few false positives. The talk closed with the announcement of a public web timeline where viewers can browse code relationships between the samples.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Tales from the SOC
talks.teaser: Two SOC investigations show how Active Directory brute force and malicious directory replication were detected and answered.
talks.summary:
Presented by two members of a Microsoft security operations center, this talk walks through two investigations from the corporate environment they monitor. The first started with an alert about brute-force attempts against many user accounts, some flagged as sensitive. The speakers explained horizontal and vertical brute force, and why simple LDAP binds, which send credentials in clear text, make such activity hard to trace from domain controller logs.

To trace the attack, the team pulled details from Windows Defender ATP and Advanced Threat Analytics, then followed the timeline on the affected machines. They found a PowerShell script disguised as an SCCM tool, opened from a shortcut file, which an employee had run for a business task. After isolating the machine and resetting the user's password, they used advanced hunting queries to search for similar command lines and checked cloud app activity for the account.

The second case involved malicious directory replication. An attacker moved laterally from a compromised account, reached a domain admin session on a machine outside the domain, and requested directory replication from a domain controller, which succeeded. Advanced Threat Analytics flagged the requests, while endpoint telemetry showed a dropped file, an unsigned binary with low prevalence, and encrypted traffic. The activity turned out to be the company's own red team. The closing advice covered unique strong passwords, secure admin workstations, application control, and monitoring replication signals, pass-the-hash, golden ticket and DCShadow activity.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Overt Command & Control: The Art of Blending In
talks.teaser: Shows how red teams blend command and control traffic into trusted cloud services to evade web proxies and blue team detection.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that defenders now run web proxies with reputation databases, EDR and threat hunting, which makes traditional HTTPS and DNS command and control easy to spot. They describe tricks their red team has used to get around these controls: buying aged domains with good reputations, domain fronting (which they say is now largely dead), and splitting traffic into smaller chunks to avoid data loss prevention. They also described persistence that survives infrastructure being burned, though each method is unreliable and new domains stand out.

The main part introduces C3, a custom command and control framework. Its implants are written in C++, with relays on compromised hosts and a server relay that passes traffic to a Cobalt Strike team server. Extensibility comes from small channel and implant interfaces, so a new transport needs only a few methods. Channels shown include OneDrive through the Graph API, Outlook tasks over REST and Exchange Web Services, and file shares for internal movement. A live demo showed a phishing payload beaconing over OneDrive, then a new file share interface reaching a second host.

In closing, the speakers said the framework would be released within weeks and suggested that defenders look for suspicious patterns in cloud service traffic, though legitimate use makes that hard. In Q&A, they acknowledged that file share relays validate commands from the server relay, but that anyone with write access could still drop files. Their core point is that defenders who use available telemetry and understand how these channels look can still detect many of them, while blending into busy cloud services makes that harder.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Mstic threat intelligence year in review
talks.teaser: A Microsoft threat intelligence team reviews a year of nation-state campaigns, takedowns, phishing and supply chain compromises.
talks.summary:
This year-in-review comes from a Microsoft threat intelligence team that tracks about 30 of roughly 132 nation-state groups full time, covering its notable cases from the past twelve months. The first case is a joint action against a North Korean group: Microsoft pushed signatures through its malicious software removal tool to delete about eight malware families from Windows machines, and it shut down well over 200 accounts, including social profiles used to approach defense industry staff. The group went quiet for about a month, then returned to cryptocurrency exchanges.

Other cases show different tactics. One group compromised internet-facing servers by exploiting an IT help desk product and dropping a web shell. A less advanced group relied on phishing, fake login pages and a Chrome extension that could read tabs and cookies, and it kept mail forwarding rules that had stayed in place for years. Another group registered for endpoint protection trials inside a victim network. The review also covers supply chain compromises, third-party remote tools used as an entry point, and commercial exploit providers serving several paying customers.

The takeaways are practical. Microsoft now notifies customers who were targeted, including those whose attacks were blocked, and aims to do this at cloud scale. The speaker stressed that credential theft and remote access tools often open the door, that password spray is hard to attribute, and that identity teams are building analytics to detect it. Attacks on industrial systems that could cause physical harm were flagged as a growing concern.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Killsuit the equation group's swiss army knife for persistence
talks.teaser: A deep walkthrough reveals how Equation Group's modular Killsuit framework enables encrypted persistence, boot kits, and covert networking.
talks.summary:
The talk centers on Killsuit, a persistence component from the Shadow Brokers' Lost in Translation leak tied to the Equation Group's DanderSpritz post-exploitation stack. The speaker frames why post-exploitation tooling drew less attention than the exploits, and outlines how FuzzBunch, DoublePulsar, and PeddleCheap lead operators to a DanderSpritz listening post where Killsuit can be deployed across several frameworks, including UnitedRake.

Killsuit is described as a modular persistence layer supporting multiple instances, kernel launchers, and an encrypted registry-backed module store. The presentation walks through persistence types such as kernel drivers, SolarTime (a VBR boot kit that hides drivers in TrueType font files), and legacy methods. Defense features include per-target encryption keys, timestamp tampering, custom TCP/IP stacks (FluxAvenue), port knocking, keyloggers, DarkSkylines packet capture, database tooling, Wi-Fi MitM (MagicBean), and FreezeRamp exfiltration. The speaker links SolarTime to Kaspersky's GrayFish reporting and touches on Quantum Shooter concepts with validators and Foxacid redirection.

Practitioners hear how survey commands enumerate safe persistence options, how research used tools like DoubleFeature and checkSOTI, and that many implant type IDs remain unexplored. The speaker shares a two-command DanderSpritz lab for hands-on study and invites the community to help reverse remaining Killsuit modules after years of adversary development versus a short public research window.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || A turla gift - popping calc.exe by sending an email
talks.teaser: A malware analyst unpacks Turla's Outlook backdoor, PDF email commands, COM persistence, and mitigations defenders can apply.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Turla's long-running APT activity, then focuses on an unusual backdoor built for the desktop Outlook client rather than web mail. Victim-owned mailboxes receive attacker emails with PDF attachments that carry encrypted command containers; the malware persists through COM object hijacking against the Outlook protocol manager, often without administrator rights, and hooks MAPI to monitor inbox and outbox folders.

The middle section walks through operational behavior: forwarding victim outbound mail, exfiltrating logs and command output inside valid-looking PDFs with data appended after a tiny JPEG, deleting traces from Sent items and suppressing UI notifications, and evolving command delivery from XML bodies to PDF blobs. Reverse engineering uncovered a heavily obfuscated container format, instruction batches protected with a modified Misty1 variant, and later in-memory PowerShell execution without powershell.exe. A lab demo showed that broken key derivation allows crafting PDFs that run arbitrary commands such as calc.exe on infected hosts.

Practitioners should treat enterprise mail clients as both delivery and control channels, hunt for COM hijacks and unsigned MAPI32 replacement, tune Windows exploit protection for Outlook child processes and code integrity guard, and consider mail-server checks and behavioral monitoring for duplicated sends to external addresses. Published white paper material and YARA guidance are pointed to for deeper IOC work.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || The matrix has you: protecting linux using deception
talks.teaser: Shows how a fault-injecting Linux honeypot with a fake shell reveals more about attacker decisions and infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how widely Linux runs in enterprises and how often it is attacked, with thousands of attempts arriving every minute. The speaker splits attackers into automated bots, script kiddies and advanced groups, and focuses on the middle group: low-skill people whose mistakes defenders can learn from. Standard high-interaction honeypots mostly reveal successful steps, leaving the attacker's decision points hidden.

The proposed alternative is a hybrid honeypot that injects deliberate faults, such as failing commands or odd system responses, so attackers take different branches and expose more of their playbook and infrastructure. The team built an SSH server in C# with a simulated Linux shell that executes nothing, randomizes the operating system it claims to be, and logs the first TCP packet to fingerprint the client's cipher suites, terminal settings and likely OS. Attacker public keys were compared against a large set of keys published on GitHub. Lures included a tar archive, presented as the required format because it carries more metadata than zip, and decoy files built to be discovered and downloaded so that stolen data can be tracked.

Reported results show unique URLs from real attackers trending up and time spent in the environment rising from about one minute to somewhat more over roughly six weeks. In a sample of 100 IP addresses, 20 to 30 percent were already known to other sources. One coin-miner case led to a later download of the lure file from separate infrastructure traced to Romania. The speaker says detection work built on this data improved by about 75 percent. The takeaway is that deception adds context beyond raw indicators, but must be designed so defenders do not create victims or get drawn into attacks.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Straight outta VMware
talks.teaser: Explains how a VMware guest's virtual graphics device can be abused to reach code execution on the Windows host.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how a guest virtual machine can reach the host through the virtual graphics device in VMware Workstation. The speaker starts with the VMware architecture: the VMX process, the kernel driver and the VMM, then the modules that set up the SVGA device. He shows how the MKS module discovers the renderer, and how guest commands travel through the SVGA3D frontend to a backend. The focus is on Windows hosts.

The middle section covers the internal objects that SVGA commands act on, including object tables, memory objects, contexts, shaders and resource containers. The speaker shows how some of these can be abused to spray the host heap, leak host memory back to the guest, and overwrite a function pointer. The case study is a public bug in the DCL_INDEXRANGE shader opcode, tracked as VMSA-2017-0006 and fixed between versions 12.5.4 and 12.5.5. He uses it to defeat ASLR and place a ROP chain.

The talk ends with a demonstration of the chain on Windows 10 against a patched VMware release. The speaker concludes that the SVGA code is fairly good but very complex, so more bugs are likely, and that VMware lacks modern exploit mitigations. A practitioner takes away reusable heap spray and leak primitives for hypervisor research.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Retpoline: The Anti sectre type 2 mitigation in windows
talks.teaser: Explains how Windows 10 implements retpoline and import optimization to mitigate Spectre variant two while preserving performance.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a condensed picture of Spectre variant two: indirect branches, branch target prediction, and cache timing let an attacker steer speculation across privilege boundaries, including into kernel address space. Retpoline is positioned against heavier options such as IBRS, which carried steep performance cost when branch prediction stayed enabled on common CPUs.

The core of the talk walks through shipping retpoline in Windows 10 (19H1). Compiler and kernel teams extended the Dynamic Value Relocation Table so metadata can mark indirect branches instead of only pointer relocations. Three branch classes receive distinct treatment: import-address retpoline with guard bitmaps and IAT indexing, generic indirect branches including CFG-aware paths, and switch-table retpoline. Import optimization replaces lingering indirect IAT calls with direct calls once the loader has finalized imports, which recovered much of the lost performance and could help even without retpoline.

Boot-time memory manager phases apply fixups before full initialization, maintain a sparse 64 KB-granularity compatibility bitmap, and patch boot and image-backed drivers with revert rules when shared pages copy into private views. Secure kernel work under HVCI required a separate implementation because normal kernel code cannot modify executable pages. Lessons include virtual stack unwinder support on trampolines, testing pain with Driver Verifier and user-mode mapping of the same driver, and querying system information to detect speculation mitigations. The closing point is that retpoline plus import optimization made Spectre v2 mitigation practical on Windows without the worst CPU penalties.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || First STRONTIUM UEFI Rootkit Unveiled
talks.teaser: Traces a Sednit-linked trojanized LoJack agent to a UEFI rootkit found in a real-world attack.
talks.summary:
ESET researchers Jean Boutin and Frederick present their analysis of a campaign attributed to the Sednit group, also tracked as Strontium and APT28. The group used a trojanized copy of the userland agent from the Computrace/LoJack anti-theft product. Earlier public research had shown that this agent's configuration was weakly protected, with a single-byte XOR key and no authentication, so an attacker who could overwrite the file could redirect the agent to a new server. Reused domains and IP addresses linked the samples to earlier Sednit operations.

Telemetry then led the team to more components. A signed kernel driver gave low-level hardware access, one tool dumped the SPI flash firmware, and a second tool inserted a rootkit called SecDxe into the UEFI image and wrote it back to flash. The writer only succeeded on misconfigured platforms, because it exploited a race condition in the BIOS write-protection logic. The rootkit dropped the agent files and temporarily changed a Windows boot-execute registry value, then restored it so the change stayed hidden.

For practitioners, the talk shows that firmware persistence survives operating system reinstalls, and that reflashing alone does not remove the userland components. Secure Boot, current firmware and modern chipset protections are the main defences, and the speakers recommend firmware assessment tools to check whether protections are configured correctly.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || An Ice Cold boot to break bitlocker
talks.teaser: Shows how cold boot memory remanence, SPI flash tampering and EFI variables can recover BitLocker keys from a powered-off laptop.
talks.summary:
Consultants tested a client's new Windows 10 laptop fleet, configured with Microsoft's recommended settings and BitLocker, against a stolen-laptop scenario. Network attacks and DMA ports were protected, so they chose a cold boot approach: chill the RAM so its contents survive power loss, then boot a separate tool to dump memory and extract the volume key.

Early dumps came back as zeroes because the firmware wiped memory at boot. Reading the SPI flash revealed a memory overwrite request flag stored in an EFI variable that is not integrity protected. The flag comes from the TCG platform reset mitigation specification, which asks firmware to wipe memory after a crash. The team built a cheap microcontroller-based programmer to clear that bit. In a recorded demo, a stolen laptop was opened, its RAM cooled, and the machine booted from USB; the volume key was recovered and the disk mounted in about two minutes. Secure Boot enrollment, boot order settings, BIOS passwords and tamper switches were also bypassed. Only a powered-off machine with a pre-boot BitLocker PIN resisted.

Takeaways: build your own threat model rather than trusting a specification, keep firmware patched, and use pre-boot PINs and shutdown policies. After a loss, revoke credentials and treat returned devices with suspicion. The vendors described physical attacks as out of scope, and hardware memory encryption was offered as a longer-term fix.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || Hardening hyper-v through offensive security research
talks.teaser: Traces a Hyper-V VM Switch race condition to host code execution, and the hardening Microsoft added afterward.
talks.summary:
This talk comes from Microsoft's offensive security research team, which writes exploits against Microsoft products to find bugs and understand the techniques behind them. It explains Hyper-V's layout: a host OS and guest VMs separated by a hypervisor, with VMBus and shared memory carrying traffic between them. The focus is VM Switch, which emulates a network card for guests and uses send and receive buffers that the host splits into sub-allocations so work can run in parallel.

The bug comes from receive buffer setup, which a guest can send more than once. Updating that buffer takes three steps with no relevant locking, so a worker thread can write data outside the intended bounds during a brief window. Malformed messages queue failing work to control timing, and a binary search finds the right count. The out-of-bounds write reaches an allocation region that held kernel stacks, which allows a return address overwrite. On Windows Server 2012 R2, an information leak from uninitialized stack data exposes code addresses, and a partial return address overwrite gets past randomization, pivoting the stack into a shared buffer.

Mitigations followed. Kernel stacks were moved out of that region, which blocks this technique and makes related overflows harder. Further hardening includes broader CFG use, shadow stack work through CET, moving more VM Switch components into the sandboxed VM worker process, and publishing symbols and Linux integration services source. A $250,000 bug bounty targets this class of exploit. A live demo, rerun after an initial failure, showed host code execution and access to other guest partitions.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || "If we win, we lose"
talks.teaser: Frames red-blue rivalry as defender-first simulation and offers metrics plus maturity cues for healthier programs.
talks.summary:
The presentation centers on a red-team mantra borrowed from NSA peers: winning an intrusion simulation can still mean organizational loss if findings are not converted into lasting defense. The speaker frames internal red teams as expensive simulated adversaries whose real job is protection, not ego-driven breaches left unfixed.

Early sections contrast productive tension with toxic red-blue dynamics, including teams that withhold fixes, repeat the same attacks without progression, or treat SOC staff as opponents rather than customers. Leadership alignment, humility, and treating blue defenders as the primary customer emerge as corrective themes, alongside habits such as sharing new tradecraft quickly and celebrating detections.

The middle develops measurement: MITRE ATT&CK coverage tracking, campaigns designed to validate detections, FAIR-style return comparisons, counting engineering projects spawned by findings, and defender-owned metrics like time to containment. A stylized maturity ladder sorts typical weaknesses—from ubiquitous credentials and weak MFA through capable SOCs to elite programs with strong egress controls and patient incident handlers.

The close argues red teams should deliberately stretch blue teams while both sides practice fundamentals relentlessly. Audience questions touch on prioritizing detection over prevention hype and inviting identity administrators into debriefs so simple chained techniques become viscerally understood.

talks.title: BlueHat v18 || DEP for the app layer - Time for app sec to grow up
talks.teaser: Contrasts perimeter WAFs with runtime instrumentation that detects injections, hardens APIs, and sandboxes dangerous interpreter paths.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that tailored security controls—Java security policies, content security policy, SELinux, and web application firewalls—rarely scale or stay maintained in production. They contrast that history with platform protections such as DEP and ASLR, which kill bug classes through the compiler and operating system without relying on every developer to master expert secure-coding habits.

They introduce runtime exploit prevention: an instrumentation agent woven into running applications to classify malicious input, trace tainted data into interpreters, perform semantic analysis on SQL and similar payloads, and block or redirect control flow when attacks crystallize. Examples include stopping obvious content-type abuse, regex denial-of-service via per-request operation counts, padding-oracle accumulation, SQL injection at execute time, tautology detection through partial evaluation, and blocking union queries against system tables. Hardening demos cover disabling external XML entities near parse calls and sandboxing OGNL so expression-language evaluation cannot reach runtime command execution, with layered chances to stop Struts-style chains that a perimeter WAF gets only one shot at.

Practitioners should treat in-process agents as the analogue of DEP for application-layer metaprogramming points: invisible to business logic, cacheable for semantic checks, and able to add mitigations before patches ship. The talk notes ecosystem limits for single-vendor runtimes versus polyglot Node stacks, and points to multi-language agent offerings while welcoming broader open-source introspection work.

talks.title: BlueHat || Exploitation Chronomancy: Temporal Return Addresses (2005)
talks.teaser: Explores using time-changing Windows memory values as predictable return addresses, and when they become usable.
talks.summary:
Matt Miller introduces temporal return addresses: memory locations holding a timer value that changes at a predictable rate, so a useful byte pattern such as a jump instruction appears at a predictable moment. He explains that exploit writers usually rely on static module addresses that shift between Windows versions, forcing version-specific targets, and that a time-based address could remove that dependence.

He describes a polling tool called telescope, which snapshots process memory at fixed intervals and flags values changing at a constant rate. From each value's capacity, period and scale, the duration of each byte position can be calculated, and viable opcodes are placed into the timer states that occur. The main case study is the system time field in the shared user data page, which sits at the same address across Windows NT versions and was executable before XP SP2 hardware NX. Its usable windows ranged from about seven minutes to days, and attacking it requires knowing the target's clock, which remote time sources can reveal.

He concludes that windows are often spaced days or months apart, null bytes limit some vectors, and the address must stay predictable and executable. Mitigations include address variation and hardware NX. He closes with the Metasploit opcode database and the idea of pooling multiple return addresses per target.

talks.title: BlueHat v17 || KERNELFAULT: R00ting the Unexploitable using Hardware Fault Injection
talks.teaser: Voltage fault injection on patched ARM Linux wins kernel memory access, root shells, and PC hijacks without any known CVE.
talks.summary:
The presenters open with fault injection basics: glitches that exploit hardware susceptibility rather than source-level bugs, common techniques including voltage fault injection, and how characterization maps delay, length, and amplitude into dead, crash, and sweet-spot regions. They connect classic secure-boot bypasses and software-activated examples such as Rowhammer-style DRAM abuse before asking whether runtime Linux on a fully patched system can be defeated the same way.

On an ARM Cortex-A9 board running Ubuntu, they glitch only the core power plane using a trigger bracketing syscalls. Thousands of automated trials show unprivileged open on /dev/mem sometimes succeeds inside a narrow microsecond window despite no known CVE, then setresuid-style calls that statistically return success and spawn a root shell within minutes. They argue duplicated software checks only raise luck requirements when attacks must hit one instant, whereas their statistical approach needs no source review.

They propose instruction corruption as a fault model beyond skip-or-flip assumptions: corrupted ARM32 destinations can land in the program counter or stack pointer, hijacking kernel flow without targeting a specific conditional. Demo video shows PC driven to a chosen address in kernel mode. They conclude software-only countermeasures often never run after a successful glitch, while control-flow and execute protections may still limit abuse; defenders should treat fault injection as a first-class threat and invest in hardware resistance.

talks.title: BlueHat v17 || Raising the Bar: New Hardware Primitives for Exploit Mitigations
talks.teaser: Explains ARMv8.3 pointer authentication, the design trade-offs behind it, and how it guards pointers against memory corruption.
talks.summary:
Rob Turner of Qualcomm presents pointer authentication, a hardware extension added in ARMv8.3 to address memory corruption in C and C++ software, where he argues that existing mitigations are not enough. He explains that a 64-bit pointer has several bits with no architectural meaning, and that these unused bits can carry an authentication code. The design had to stay transparent to developers, work for both application and system code, interoperate with legacy binaries, and add no extra tag memory.

The talk then covers the instruction groups that compute and verify these codes, and how a failed check leaves an invalid pointer that faults when dereferenced, so the failure can be identified afterwards. The speaker explains why authentication was preferred over encryption, citing error detection, debugging with core dumps, and keeping speculative execution fed. The QARMA tweakable cipher and its five 128-bit keys are described. The security analysis looks at guessing and forging, attackers with arbitrary read and write, and pointer substitution attacks, where pointers signed with the same key and context are interchangeable. A trade-off is that a smaller address space yields more authentication bits.

To close, the speaker shows return address protection that uses the stack pointer as context and is cheaper than software stack-smashing protection. He suggests similar uses in import tables, C library jump buffers, and operating system pointer-encoding APIs. The takeaway is that the primitive helps build mitigations but does not stop data-only attacks, so practitioners should decide which pointers to protect and use context as widely as possible.

talks.title: BlueHat v17 || Betraying the BIOS: Where the Guardians of the BIOS are Failing
talks.teaser: Explains how UEFI update flaws and misconfigured Intel Boot Guard let attackers persist in PC firmware.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why firmware protections meant to secure the PC boot process keep failing in practice. The speaker argues that BIOS and UEFI update paths are an attractive route for attackers who already have kernel access, since they can reach System Management Mode handlers that write to the SPI flash. Many vendors, he says, skip write-protection bits, leave flash regions unprotected or do not verify update signatures, and several handlers he reviewed were open to simple callout attacks.

The middle of the talk focuses on Intel Boot Guard, the hardware-anchored root of trust. The speaker walks through how the initial boot block manifest, its hashes and the authenticated code modules are checked, and shows that some vendors enable Boot Guard without BIOS Guard or leave its fuses unlocked. On a sixth-generation Skylake board, he presented a bypass that combined write access to the Intel ME region with an unlocked Boot Guard configuration, allowing the firmware to be altered.

He closes with practical advice: check firmware settings on hardware before it reaches data centers, keep BIOS updates current, and confirm that Boot Guard is both enabled and locked rather than assumed. He also released a tool for verifying UEFI firmware volumes and said that the Surface implementation was stronger than most others he examined.

talks.title: BlueHat v17 || Dangerous Contents
talks.teaser: Explains how insecure .NET deserialization enables code execution and outlines prevention and scanning steps.
talks.summary:
Serialization turns in-memory objects into a stream that can be stored or sent and later rebuilt. The talk explains why this becomes dangerous in .NET: several deserializers read type names from the incoming data, so anyone who can alter that data can make the program create unexpected types. Framework types with side-effecting constructors, setters or finalizers can be chained into gadgets. A simple example used TempFileCollection with BinaryFormatter, where a crafted object deletes files when it is garbage collected.

Several APIs are covered. BinaryFormatter is the most common risk and sits underneath features such as ASP.NET ViewState and resource files. JavaScriptSerializer is safe by default but becomes exploitable with a simple type resolver, and a payload that builds an XmlDocument can enable file disclosure or server-side request forgery. Json.NET with a non-default TypeNameHandling setting can bridge into BinaryFormatter through a WindowsIdentity gadget. ServiceStack.Text can be walked to a member of type object, and its later allow list still included every serializable class by default.

Attacks need three conditions: a stream an attacker can modify, type information read from that stream, and no limit on the types created. Mitigations include keeping streams server-side or protecting them with an HMAC, preferring DataContractSerializer or XmlSerializer, and writing exact-match SerializationBinder allow lists that throw on unexpected types. ASP.NET machine keys should be guarded like admin passwords. To find exposure, search source code for TypeNameHandling and SimpleTypeResolver, and check web logs for base64 prefixes or $type markers.

talks.title: BlueHat v17 || Born Secure. How to Design A Brand New Cloud Platform With A Strong Security Posture
talks.teaser: Shows how Azure Stack was built as a sealed, hardened platform with security designed in from the ground up.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how a cloud platform can be designed with security built in from the start, using Azure Stack as the example. Because the vendor controls the hardware, software and deployment, the team could apply a hardened baseline based on DISA STIG instead of inheriting legacy defaults. Measures described include requiring secure boot and TPM 2.0, BitLocker on infrastructure and storage, TLS 1.2 only, removal of unneeded components, and rotating group managed service account passwords every 24 hours.

The central theme is limiting administrator power and assuming breach. Administration goes through three entry points: a portal, the Azure Resource Manager API, and a privileged endpoint built on PowerShell just enough administration for support. In a live demo, a constrained session blocked Mimikatz and an unsigned Chrome installer under code integrity policy, and Defender and code integrity events were logged as attack signals. Network whitelisting at the host, software-defined network and switch layers limits lateral movement, and support sessions need a two-person unlock involving the customer and Microsoft.

The closing part covers detection, patching and compliance. Logs from all components are stored centrally and exposed through a REST interface so partners can feed them into a SIEM. Orchestrated updates keep customers within a three-month patching window, and OEM hardware partners must meet the same security requirements. Compliance controls were built into the infrastructure, with a third-party assessment started for standards such as PCI, while people and process controls remain with the customer.

talks.title: BlueHat v17 || Don't Let Your Virtualization Fabric Become the Attack Vector
talks.teaser: Walks through fabric-admin attacks on virtual machines and the layered Hyper-V defenses that block them.
talks.summary:
Dean Wells, a Windows Server program manager, examines attacks that exist only because workloads run on a virtualization fabric, where whoever administers the hosts can often reach the virtual machines on them. The examples centre on Hyper-V, but he argues the techniques apply to other hypervisors too. A storage admin and a fabric admin serve as fictional attackers in a sequence of escalating steps.

Early attacks copy a virtual domain controller's disk and pull password hashes from it, and keys held by the host for disk encryption only shift the problem to the fabric admin. Later, a malicious boot ISO imitates the BitLocker passphrase prompt to capture the passphrase, and a memory dump taken with a live debugger yields the volume encryption key. Moving aside the compiled code integrity policy file works until the policy is locked in a UEFI secure variable, and a full host crash dump is stopped by encrypting dumps and requiring health attestation before keys are released.

The takeaway is that fabric administration should not imply access to workload secrets. The speaker lists the building blocks needed: guest UEFI secure and measured boot, a virtual TPM, signed template disks, hypervisor-enforced code integrity, encrypted crash dumps and state files, and key release tied to attestation. He closes by noting that the attestation service is the main deployment hurdle for customers.

talks.title: BlueHat v17 || Scaling Incident Response - 5 Keys to Successful Defense at Scale
talks.teaser: Explains how incident response can scale to a fleet of 200,000 machines using inventory, forensics, IOC matching and fleet-wide jobs.
talks.summary:
Matt Swan, whose team secures customer data in SharePoint Online and Office 365, explains why traditional incident response stops working at cloud scale. Running scripts across domains and querying event logs in Cosmos or HDInsight no longer keeps up when the fleet reaches over 200,000 machines and the logs reach terabytes per day. He presents five capabilities his team built to close that gap.

The early capabilities focus on visibility. A lightweight agent answers queries on each machine on a randomized schedule and reports to a cloud database, enabling historical tracking of fleet health. Agents also scan their local /24 subnets to find unmanaged Windows hosts, and that inventory can drive automated remediation and firewall configuration. For forensics, agents upload startup entries, local groups and certificates daily, and attach a snapshot of logged-in users, processes and loaded DLLs to real-time alerts. Executables go through a cloud workflow that runs PE Studio triage.

The later capabilities focus on hunting and eviction. An IOC store fed by findings from real incidents syncs to agents every 15 minutes, and a job system runs YARA scans across the fleet. In a red team exercise, new indicators produced a feedback loop that surfaced additional command and control infrastructure. For response, the team applied coordinated inoculation such as static routes, hosts file sinkholes and blocked image execution, and normalized data into Kusto with a shared schema so queries can span tables. He added that IP blackholing was still being built and needs guards against overly broad blocks.

talks.title: BlueHat v17 || Mitigations for the Masses: From EMET to Windows Defender Exploit Guard
talks.teaser: Shows how EMET's mitigations moved into Windows 10 as Exploit Guard, with attack surface rules and a Firefox exploit walkthrough.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how Microsoft retired the Enhanced Mitigation Experience Toolkit (EMET) and how its useful protections were carried into Windows 10 as Windows Defender Exploit Guard. The presenters explain why EMET was ended: it had been built outside the core Windows engineering process, the faster Windows release cadence and built-in mitigations such as Control Flow Guard had overtaken it, and legacy applications that could not be recompiled still needed protection. That gap shaped the new feature set.

The middle of the session covers the two main components. Attack surface reduction (ASR) rules block behaviour patterns rather than specific modules, and the speakers illustrate this with Office documents that launch child processes, using a DDE-based delivery chain that ends in ransomware. Exploit protection provides a central interface for per-application mitigations. A Firefox use-after-free exploit is then walked through step by step, showing where import address filtering, export address filtering and anti-ROP checks would each catch it, with event log output and a live demo configured through the UI and PowerShell.

The closing part explains the audit mode workflow, where rule hits are written to the Windows event log and forwarded to Defender ATP before enforcement is switched on. In the Q&A, the presenters confirmed that third parties cannot add new mitigations to the operating system. The practical takeaway is to test ASR rules and exploit mitigations in audit mode before enforcing them on legacy applications.

talks.title: BlueHat v17 || Keynote: Reinventing Trust in a World of Organized Chaos
talks.teaser: Keynote examines rebuilding trust through transparency, coordinated incident response, and automated threat information sharing.
talks.summary:
Eroding trust in vendors, devices, and headlines sits at the center of this general-audience keynote. Daily breaches, routing incidents, and waves of renamed jargon leave operators unsure what to believe. The speaker argues that durable security still maps to authentication, authorization, integrity, confidentiality, and availability, while automation has scaled attacks from early denial-of-service bursts to vast botnets and stealthy traffic shaping.

The middle of the talk walks home and enterprise risk: connected appliances with opaque behavior, cloud dependence without clear data custody, mobile backup paths, social oversharing, certification limits, and phishing that fools even careful practitioners. Regulation such as GDPR is portrayed as forcing overdue access reviews. Information sharing remains legally fraught for defenders while adversaries collaborate freely; machine-to-machine exchange frameworks and policy work aim to lower those barriers.

Closing themes tie trust to incident response rather than spectacle. Estonia’s 2007 attacks and later national ID card cryptographic flaws illustrate transparent government communication, international help, and large-scale remediation without panic. Equifax-style pile-ons and breathless English-language reporting are contrasted with measured fixes. Practitioners are urged to favor transparency, cross-border cooperation, automation where users cannot reliably judge URLs, personal responsibility for mistakes, and cryptography without backdoors.
